activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
knowledge_domain: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
fact: Properly tempered chocolate shrinks slightly as it sets, which helps it release cleanly from a mould.
story:
The moulds had belonged to Ms. Campbell-Brown, who had left them at the door in a plastic bag with a note that said only, "For your project. Return whenever." Rosalie set them on the kitchen counter beside the double boiler, the thermometer, and the three bars of dark chocolate she had bought with her own money, and she told herself that this time she would not improvise. Her mother was at work until seven, which gave her the house to itself: the radio off, the windows shut against the August heat, the air conditioner grumbling in the corner like an unwilling accomplice.

She was making these chocolates for Elise's going-away party, twenty-four small shells that had to look like something a person would want to eat, not like evidence of a struggle. The first attempt, two nights ago, had ended in disaster. She had melted the chocolate, poured it into the moulds, cooled it in the fridge, and then spent forty minutes prying the shells out with a butter knife while they bloomed grey streaks and cracked along the edges. Elise had texted her a photo of her own batch, glossy and uniform, with the caption "no big deal," and Rosalie had stared at it for a long time before deciding that it was, in fact, a big deal.

So tonight she was following the method properly. Melt to the right temperature, cool it down on a marble slab she had borrowed along with everything else, work it with the spatula until it thickened and lost its sheen, then warm it gently back. The science of it, as far as she could gather, was about the crystals in the cocoa butter, though the more she read the less the explanations seemed to agree. Erik, when she had described her plan to him, had offered to expatiate on crystal structures for as long as she liked, and she had declined, on the grounds that she wanted to make chocolate, not write a thesis about it.

The work was slower than she expected. Stirring the melted chocolate on the slab, she kept one eye on the thermometer and the other on the clock, because Elise's party was Saturday and tonight was Thursday and there was no room left for another failure. The chocolate cooled in her hands' rhythm, thickening, dragging against the marble. When she brought it back over the warm water, it loosened into something liquid but not runny, and when she dipped the tip of a knife in it and waited thirty seconds, it set with a dull snap. She thought that was supposed to mean something. She was not entirely sure what.

She poured the moulds, tapped each one on the counter to chase out the bubbles, and slid them into the cool pantry, not the fridge, because one of the forums had insisted that rushing the setting caused the streaks. Then she cleaned the kitchen, because evidence of a struggle was still evidence, and waited. Waiting was the part no one wrote about. She sat at the table with her chemistry notes in front of her and did not read them, and she thought about how she had spent three years in school collecting facts the way other people collected stamps, sorting them into a private taxonomy of things known and things guessed, and how none of that sorting had ever made her as nervous as twenty-four chocolate shells sitting in a dark pantry.

When she turned the first mould over an hour later, nothing happened. She tapped it. Nothing. She felt the old frustration rising, the butter knife already in her mind, and then she stopped, because something was different. The chocolate had shrunk. She could see it, a hair's width of daylight between the shells and the sides of the mould, all the way around, each shell sitting slightly loose in its cavity. The first batch had gripped the plastic like it had been welded there. This batch had drawn back from it.

She held the mould over the counter and flexed it, gently, and the shells dropped out one after another, clean-edged, glossy, whole. She picked one up and snapped it in half, and it broke with a sound like a small click, bright and definite, nothing like the crumble of the failed batch. That, she realized, was what the knife test had been telling her: the chocolate that shrinks as it sets is the chocolate in temper, and the chocolate in temper is the chocolate that lets go. She was not sure she could explain the whole chain of it, and she suspected that if she tried, Erik would correct her on some point of crystal structure, but she understood it in her hands, which for the moment felt like the more reliable organ.

She dipped a half-shell in the leftover chocolate and ate it, standing at the counter, and then she wrapped the others in the paper she had bought and stacked them in a tin, and she took a photograph before she could talk herself out of it. She sent it to Elise with no caption at all. Then she carried the moulds, still faintly fragrant, to the sink to wash them for the next batch, because if one clean release proved anything it did not prove everything, and she wanted to know whether she could do it twice.

The reply from Elise arrived while the water was running: "how. tell me everything tomorrow." Rosalie typed "might show you," set the phone face-down on the counter, and went back to the moulds, turning them over in the steam to check for scratches, and finding none.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: The Islamic calendar is lunar and about 10 to 11 days shorter than the solar year, so Ramadan and Eid al-Fitr come roughly 10 to 11 days earlier each year.
story:
I told Layne I wasn't going to the festival, which was a lie I had already committed to, so by Thursday I'd almost believed it myself. The truth was that my mother had promised my aunt we would come to the Eid gathering on Delancey, and the truth underneath that was that I wanted to go and didn't want Layne to know I wanted to, because Layne had said, at lunch, in that flat voice she used when she was daring you, "So you're just skipping the calc review." I wasn't skipping it. I had it in my bag, photocopied, folded twice.

The street smelled like fried dough and cardamom. Lanterns were strung between the lampposts, and my little cousins ran under them screaming in a mix of English and my grandmother's dialect, which I only half understood, which I pretended to understand fully. My aunt pressed a plate of sheer khurma into my hands and said, "Eat, you're too thin," which is what she says every year, about everyone, and every year I am apparently exactly the same amount of thin. I sat on the curb and did not open my bag. The review could delimit what I knew and what I didn't, but it couldn't tell me which of those mattered more, the exam or this.

That's how I remember it, anyway.

Layne's messages came in around eight, and I have them still, so this part at least is exact. "did you seriously go." Then: "exam is the 14th. ms mendoza moved the review to saturday morning." Then: "you said you weren't going." I typed and deleted three answers before my cousin Hamza, six years old and merciless, leaned over my shoulder and read the screen aloud at volume. I put the phone face down on the concrete and let it buzz itself torpid, if a phone can be torpid, which it can't, but it lay there inert while the speakers up the block started a song my mother swayed to with her eyes closed.

Kalvin found me there, because Kalvin finds everyone, an aesthete of street food who had already eaten at four stalls and ranked them aloud. "Layne's furious," he said, sitting down uninvited. "She thinks you lied."

"I didn't lie. Plans changed."

"Plans changed when?" He was eating something on a stick, gesturing with it. "Ari. The exam's the fourteenth. That's the thing. She just realized Eid is like, during exam week, and she's mad that the universe did that to her, and you're a convenient universe."

"I don't follow."

"She thought Eid was a summer thing. She saw your photos from last year, the July ones. Now it's May and she's convinced someone moved it."

"Somebody did move it," I said. "Not somebody. The calendar. The Islamic calendar is lunar, and it's about ten to eleven days shorter than the solar year. So Ramadan and Eid come roughly ten to eleven days earlier every year." I'd learned that at eleven, from my father, sitting exactly on this curb, and I'd forgotten it and relearned it every year since, the way you relearn a relative's name.

Kalvin chewed on this longer than he chewed the food. "So it just walks backward through the year? Forever?"

"Ten or eleven days earlier. Every year. Last summer, this spring, and in a few years it'll be midwinter." He looked at me like I'd told him the streetlights were load-bearing. "Your whole school calendar is built on the sun," I said. "Ours isn't."

Layne, it turned out, had not been furious. This is where I have to admit I got her wrong the entire evening, standing in line for falooda, composing defenses. From Layne's side, which I know because she showed me her drafts later, unrevised and unrevisable, she had spent that hour writing and deleting not accusations but something closer to an apology: "i didn't know eid moved like that. nobody ever told me. i didn't mean to make you choose." She never sent it. What she sent was "you said you weren't going," and I sent back nothing, and the nothing sat between us all night like a fourth person.

My mother came to collect me at ten, glowing from dancing, my aunt behind her carrying foil-wrapped plates for people who hadn't come. On the walk to the car she asked if I'd studied, and I said some, which was a lie, and she nodded as though it were true, as though the nod could make it so. At the corner my phone buzzed once more. I read it under the last lantern before the string went dark.

"saturday review, 9 am. i saved you a seat. don't be an idiot about it."

activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
knowledge_domain: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
fact: Brown nitrogen dioxide forms colourless dinitrogen tetroxide in an exothermic reaction, so a sealed tube of the gas turns paler when cooled and darker brown when warmed.
story:
Katherine set the two sealed tubes on the kitchen counter beside a bowl of ice water and the kettle her mother kept for tea, and told herself that if this went wrong it would only be wrong in front of Cassidy and Isaak, which was a limited kind of humiliation. Mr. Sutherland had lent her the tubes from the chemistry storeroom after she stayed behind on Thursday, spinning her pen and admitting she could not make equilibrium feel real. "It's the word shifting that loses me," she had said. "Everything else in chemistry has a direction. This just leans." He had looked at her for a moment, dour as ever, then unlocked the cabinet.

The gas inside the tubes was brown, a deep amber-brown like strong tea held up to the window. Cassidy arrived first, dropping her bag by the fridge, and Isaak came ten minutes later with his boots still wet from the bus stop. He leaned over the tubes and tapped the glass with one fingernail. "It's like someone bottled rust," he said. "Whose house is this actually legal in?"

"Mr. Sutherland's," Katherine said. "He signed them out to me. There's a worksheet too, which I'm ignoring, because the worksheet is what confused me in the first place." She took a breath. "Watch the left one."

She lowered the first tube into the ice water and held it there, and for a moment nothing happened, long enough that Cassidy said, gently, "Kat, it's just sitting there." Then the colour began to thin. The brown faded from the bottom of the tube upward, going watery, then almost clear, until the gas above the ice bath was paler than the gas in the second tube the way weak tea is paler than strong. Cassidy put her face level with the counter. "It's disappearing. Where does it go?"

"Nowhere," Katherine said, and pulled the kettle, which she'd already boiled, toward a mug of hot water she'd prepared. "It turns into something you can't see. Brown nitrogen dioxide, colourless dinitrogen tetroxide. The two change into each other, back and forth, and the brown one forms the colourless one in an exothermic reaction, so it lets out heat when it goes that way." She had practiced the sentence on the bus until it stopped sounding recited. "Cold pushes it toward the colourless side. Watch."

She lifted the pale tube out of the ice bath and plunged it into the hot water, and the brown came back like a tide, darkening until the tube sat beside its twin almost indistinguishable, two columns of the same deep colour. Isaak, who had gone quiet in the way he did when something actually interested him, said, "So heat doesn't just make things faster. It decides which way it leans."

"That's the part I kept getting wrong," Katherine said. "I kept thinking of temperature like the other things, concentration, pressure, like a weight you add to one side of a scale. But heat is different because the reaction itself makes heat or swallows it, so the temperature is inside the balance, not outside it." She was aware of Cassidy watching her, and aware that she was talking faster than she meant to, the way she did when two ideas she had been holding apart finally touched. "In class I wanted one rule that covered everything, and Mr. Sutherland kept saying it depends, which used to sound like he was dodging. It's not dodging. The rule is that everything shifts to counter what you did, and temperature is just the case where what you did and what the reaction is are tangled together." She caught herself. "Sorry. I sound like the textbook."

"You sound like someone who finally gets it," Cassidy said. "Which is more than the textbook ever did for me."

Katherine turned the dark tube in her fingers, and the colour moved with it, unbroken. There was still something she could not claim to fully hold: why the universe arranged itself so that a system pushed back against every push, whether that was a fact about molecules or a habit of description, a way chemists had of contextualizing what they could not quite see. She did not say any of this. She was learning to let a thing be half-understood without feeling it was lost. Instead she set both tubes back in the ice water, side by side, and said, "Count to sixty with me and we'll see if they pale together."

activity: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
knowledge_domain: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
fact: In a fixed-payment loan, each payment's interest is charged on the remaining balance, so early payments go more toward interest and later payments more toward principal.
story:
The flyer was taped to the gym door by first period: student parking permits, forty dollars, cash or check, due Friday. Ava read it twice, because she had been saving since September toward a car, a gray hatchback with a dented fender that her neighbor was selling for two thousand dollars. She had eleven hundred. The gap had a way of sitting in her mind during class, patient and heavy, like a stone in a pocket.

At lunch she spread her savings notebook on the cafeteria table, the pages soft from handling. Lennon slid in across from her with a tray and leaned over the columns of numbers. "You're still tracking every dollar?" Lennon asked. Ava showed her the latest page: twelve dollars from tutoring on Tuesday, five from returning bottles, a birthday fifty from an aunt recorded in April and, beneath it, the running interest line from the credit union's youth account. "It grows a little on itself," Ava said. "Every month the interest gets added, and then the next month's interest is on the bigger amount, so it grows faster than I expected. It's slow, but it speeds up." Lennon squinted at the small numbers as if they might be hiding something.

That afternoon, Ms. Gallagher kept her after fifth period to return a paper, and while Ava waited she noticed a printed loan statement on the corner of the desk, folded back to a payment history. Ms. Gallagher saw her looking and, instead of covering it, turned it toward her. "My car," Ms. Gallagher said. "Three years in, and I still owe more than I thought I would." She tapped a column with one finger. "Every payment, the interest is charged on the remaining balance. So early on, when the balance is biggest, most of the payment goes to interest. Later, more of it goes to the actual loan." She said it flatly, the way people recite things they learned the hard way, and then went back to the paper in her hand, leaving the statement where Ava could see it.

Ava looked at the columns. The early payments had knocked the balance down by almost nothing; the recent ones bit deeper. She thought of her own notebook, the mirror image, the interest arriving on a growing remainder instead of a shrinking one. The two systems sat in her mind side by side, and she turned them over like coins from different countries, wondering whether they were truly opposites or just the same machine running in different directions, one quietly building and one quietly taking. She did not have an answer, only the noticing.

She walked home by way of the credit union. The cashier at the counter was young and unhurried, so Ava asked about the loan side of things, the rates posted on the wall, what a small loan would cost. The cashier walked her through a sample payment book, and there it was again, the same shape Ms. Gallagher's statement had shown: the balance barely moving at first, the interest eating the early payments because it was charged on what was still owed. Ava thanked her and stood outside for a minute in the cold, doing arithmetic against the glass.

The numbers said this: if she borrowed the missing nine hundred at the posted rate to get the hatchback now, the two thousand would transmute into something like twenty-two hundred over the life of the loan, and the first months would feel like shoveling sand. The alternative was to wait, to keep the eleven hundred earning its small compounding interest, and the gap would close not by her deposits alone but by the deposits plus what they earned plus what the earnings earned, a sedimentary thing, layer on thin layer, slow and then not slow.

She was honest with herself about the uncertainty. She did not know how much longer the neighbor would keep the car, or whether the transmission that made the faint clicking sound would last. She did not know whether Ms. Gallagher, at the start of her loan, had known what the payment book would do, or whether knowing would have changed anything. Solvency, Ava understood from the flyer crumpled in her pocket, was not just having money but having enough that the machine worked for you instead of against you, and she was standing, right now, exactly on the line between the two.

At dinner she laid both versions in front of her mother: borrow and drive, or wait and watch the interest work in her favor for once. Her mother asked what the payment would be, and what the total would come to, and Ava had the figures ready, columns of them, and also the thing the figures sat inside. "The interest is charged on what's left," Ava said. "So the early payments mostly don't touch the loan itself. You're paying for the borrowing before you're paying off the car." Her mother put down her fork.

Later, at the kitchen table, Ava opened the notebook to a fresh page and drew a line down the middle. On the left she wrote "borrow now" and listed the costs in her small careful hand; on the right she wrote "wait" and copied the savings column, then extended it three months forward, then six, the interest line thickening almost imperceptibly as it went. She sat with her pen above the page. The hatchback was in the driveway next door, gray under the porch light, and from the kitchen window she could see its dented fender, and she could see, too, that the light had been left on inside it.

activity: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
knowledge_domain: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
fact: Two parallel plates 0.02 metres apart with 100 volts across them produce an electric field of 5,000 volts per metre between them.
story:
Ella sat at the kitchen table with her physics worksheet, a pencil, and her father's old calculator, the one with the cracked corner and the division sign worn almost smooth. The third problem asked for the electric field strength at a point between two parallel plates. The plates were 0.02 metres apart, the book said, and there were 100 volts across them. She had been on this problem for twenty minutes, and the problem before it had taken her forty.

The house was quiet except for the refrigerator. Her mother was at work until nine, and the plan, agreed on that morning, was that Ella would finish the worksheet before dinner and then go to Elyssa's to watch a movie. That was the want that kept her at the table. She copied the numbers onto a fresh line of scrap paper and divided, and got 0.02, which she wrote in the answer blank, and then crossed out, because the blank wanted units and she did not know what the units were.

She texted Joy. "do you know what the units for electric field strength are." Joy texted back a photo of her own worksheet, unfinished, with "help" written across the top in capital letters. Then Elyssa called, because Elyssa never used fewer words than a phone call required.

"You divide the volts by the distance," Elyssa said. "It's volts per metre. Mr. Watanabe said it like five times on Tuesday, when you were drawing on your shoe."

"Volts per metre," Ella repeated. She looked at her crossed-out answer. Two hundred volts divided by two centimetres was one hundred. Her answer of 0.02 had come from somewhere else entirely, a division she had set up wrong and then followed down the page like a path into a field.

"So what did you get," Elyssa said.

"One hundred. That's volts per centimetre, though. That's not the unit."

"Then make it the unit. Convert."

Ella sat with the phone against her shoulder and thought about her grandfather, who had been a raconteur at every family dinner, retelling the same three stories about the river, and who had once spent a whole afternoon teaching her to convert inches to centimetres with a wooden ruler and a length of fishing line. He had been patient in a way that made you patient too. She had not thought of him in months, and now she thought of him while she rewrote the distance. Two centimetres was 0.02 metres. The plates were not two metres apart, obviously, and they were not two millimetres apart either. She had seen the apparatus in class, the two grey plates with the gap you could put a fingertip in.

She divided 100 volts by 0.02 metres and got 5,000.

"Five thousand volts per metre," she said into the phone.

"That's what I got for the same problem," Elyssa said. "Wait, yours is the same problem? The two centimetre plates?"

"The 0.02 metre plates," Ella said. "Which are the same plates."

"My first answer was fifty," Elyssa said. "I forgot to convert the centimetres too. I divided 100 by 2 and then stopped, because it looked done."

Ella wrote 5,000 V/m in the blank and boxed it, then checked the number against her scrap paper twice, because a hundredfold error could hide anywhere and she wanted to be sure it had not hidden in her arithmetic. Her earlier answer had been wrong by more than an order of magnitude, which meant wrong in the way that mattered. She tried to introspect on how it had happened, whether it was carelessness or something structural in how she read problems, and she could not decide, and decided that was honest. She wrote 0.02 m at the top of her work so that anyone reading it could follow.

They stayed on the phone while Elyssa redid her own page. Outside, the light was going the flat grey of late afternoon, and the dirt of the flowerbed her mother had dug last month had settled into a smooth, alluvial slope against the fence. Ella finished the last two problems, which were about points between the plates and wanted the same number she had already found, and closed the workbook.

"Come over at seven instead of six," Elyssa said. "I still have three problems."

"I'll bring the worksheet," Ella said, and put the calculator down on the table, squared to the edge, the way her grandfather used to leave his tools.

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: The US National Safety Council recommends a following distance of at least three seconds, adding a second for each difficulty such as bad weather or heavy traffic.
story:
The parking lot behind the shuttered Kmart had been Sofia's idea, because Sofia had ideas the way other people had loose change, constantly and without much thought. Justine's mother sat in the passenger seat with the seatbelt crossed twice over her cardigan, the way she crossed everything, and Sofia folded herself into the back with her phone already out. Rain had come through an hour ago and left the asphalt glittering under the one working light, so that the lot looked less like a place for learning and more like a place for something that had already happened.

"Three seconds," her mother said, before Justine had even touched the ignition. "You count the car in front of you passing a marker, and you should pass it no less than three seconds later. That's what the National Safety Council says. At least three."

Sofia leaned between the seats. "Two is fine. Erika does two and she's had her license for like four months."

"Erika has four months of being lucky," her mother said, and then, in a softer register Justine knew was meant to be private, "Three, Justine. Humor me."

The car lurched twice before Justine found the friction point, and the third time it stalled, Sofia laughed without malice, which was somehow worse. Her mother said nothing. Her mother had spent sixteen years trying to inculcate patience in Justine through demonstration, and the demonstration was failing, because Justine's hands were shaking on the wheel and the rain was starting again, fine and sideways, blurring the light into long smears across the windshield.

On the fourth attempt the engine caught and held, and the car moved, and something in Justine's chest loosened and then immediately tightened again, because movement was not the same as control. She circled the lot at ten miles an hour, hugging the painted lines, and her mother talked her through the turn at the far end where a shopping cart had been abandoned like a small monument. Sofia narrated from the back seat, an imaginary passenger, then an imaginary pedestrian, then, regrettably, an imaginary squirrel, and Justine laughed and drifted wide and overcorrected and felt the wheel go loose and strange in her palms.

"Okay, stop," her mother said. Not angry. Just final. She had Justine pull up beside the cart, and they sat with the wipers ticking, and the rain thickened against the glass. "Now think. It's raining. The road is wet. What does that change?"

Justine looked at the lot, at the pooled water spreading black and thin across the asphalt. She thought of Sofia's two seconds, so casual, so confident, and of her mother's three, delivered like scripture. And she understood, suddenly, that neither of them had said the whole thing, that her mother had stopped before the part that mattered. "You said at least three," Justine said slowly. "And you add a second for each difficulty. So rain would be a difficulty. That's four."

Her mother was quiet a moment. The wipers ticked. "Where did you get that?"

"You. Just now. You said at least three, like there was more, and it's raining, so." She heard how thin it sounded. "Four seconds when it's raining. Or heavy traffic. Each thing that's hard, you add a second."

Her mother turned in her seat, and there was something in her face Justine couldn't read, an expression her perspicacity failed her on completely, and then her mother said, "Yes. That's exactly right," and Justine felt the compliment land somewhere complicated, because it hadn't come from being good at this, only from listening to the gap in a sentence.

"Four seconds," Sofia said from the back, in the tone of someone filing information for later, possibly for an argument with Erika. Then, brighter, the want surfacing the way it always did: "Can I get out and be the car in front? I'll walk, you follow me, you count. Come on. I want to be part of it, not just luggage."

Her mother hesitated, and Justine, surprising herself, said, "Let her." Sofia jogged out into the rain in her thin jacket, hair flattening immediately, and took up a position thirty feet ahead, arms out, a small dark figure on the shining asphalt. Justine watched her pass the shopping cart, counted one, two, three, four, and eased the car past the same cart as the fourth second broke. Behind her in the mirror, Sofia was grinning and soaked and turning around to walk back, thumbs up, a driver's-ed angel in a ruined denim jacket, and Justine held the brake and the wheel and the moment together, knowing her mother would take the keys soon, knowing tomorrow she would have to do it all again on a real street with real cars driven by people who had never met her, and still, for exactly four seconds, following no one, going nowhere, she was driving.

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
knowledge_domain: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
fact: A few drops of water in melted chocolate can make it seize into a thick, grainy paste, because the sugar and cocoa particles clump together.
story:
The kitchen of the Marigold had a smell Morgan could not stop noticing, roasted garlic underneath something darker, almost earthy, which she learned on her first Saturday was cocoa warming in the back corner where the pastry station lived. Ms. Li, who owned the place and worked the sauté line like a conductor, had agreed to let her spend the spring watching the dessert prep, and Morgan had said yes before her mother could ask a single practical question about wages or hours. She wanted to know how things worked, and chocolate, she was discovering, worked in ways nobody had ever bothered to tell her.

"Tempering," Ms. Li said that first morning, sliding a bowl of dark callets across the steel counter. "You melt it, you cool it, you warm it again just a little. Do it right and it sets shiny and it snaps when you break it. Do it wrong and you get something dull that bends." She said it the way she said everything, plainly, as if the sentence were a tool she was handing over rather than a lesson she was teaching. Then she went back to her pans and left Morgan alone with the bowl, the thermometer, and the double boiler.

Zachariah, who washed dishes and had, he claimed, opinions about everything, leaned over the partition between the dish pit and the pastry corner. "It's all about the crystals," he said. "There's like six kinds and only one of them is the good one." Morgan asked him which one, and he shrugged, delighted to have been asked and deflated to have no answer. Harris, who bused tables and had applied to six colleges, four of which had already said no, wandered through with a tub of cutlery and said the whole thing sounded like chemistry, which he had failed, and therefore respected.

Morgan set the water simmering and balanced the bowl above it, careful the way Ms. Li had shown her, the bottom of the bowl not touching the water, because wet chocolate was ruined chocolate. She had heard that without believing it much. How could a few drops of anything matter in a whole bowl? She stirred in slow figure eights and watched the callets soften and slacken into something glossy and liquid, and she thought about how the same chocolate had been hard and matte an hour ago, and would be again, and the difference was not really the temperature but some arrangement inside it she could not see. That was the part that kept her stirring past the point where stirring was needed.

It happened on the second Saturday. She had the bowl too low, or the water too high, and a bead of condensation gathered under the rim and let go, and then another, and the drops fell into the chocolate while her back was turned toward Harris, who was telling a long story about a florid letter his coach had sent home, full of words like "unacceptable" and "character." When Morgan turned back and stirred, the chocolate fought her. It went stiff in three seconds, thickening from a silky pour into a grainy paste that clung to the spatula in a clump. She stood very still, the way you do when something breaks.

"It seized," Zachariah said from the dish pit, peering over with soap to his elbows. "Water does that. Just a few drops and the sugar and cocoa all clump together." He said it without any satisfaction, which she appreciated, and then he went back to his sprayer, leaving her with the ruined bowl and the strange fact that something so small could undo something so careful.

She scooped the stiff mass into a container and labeled it, and then, because throwing it out felt like an ending and she was not sure it deserved one, she asked Ms. Li whether it was dead. Ms. Li poked it with a spoon. "For this, yes. You can bake with it. But it won't ever set right now." She did not eulogize the bowl or the afternoon, did not sigh over wasted chocolate, and somehow that restraint made Morgan feel the loss more, and also less, because a mistake that nobody dramatized was a mistake you could simply study.

What she studied, over the next few weekends, was her own disagreement with herself. Harris thought the answer was precision, more thermometers, less talking, a rule for everything, and he argued for it with the fervor of someone rehearsing for the adult he intended to become. Zachariah thought the answer was feel, that hands learned what numbers could not, and that Ms. Li never looked at a thermometer when she tempered, only at the edge of the chocolate as it thickened against the bowl. Morgan found she could not choose between them, and more than that, did not want to. The thermometer told her when she was close; the way the chocolate sheeted off the spatula told her when she was there. Two vocabularies for one truth, she thought, and neither one lying, and she tested the idea by tempering a batch with the thermometer alone, then a batch by eye. The second snapped cleaner. She wrote that down in the small notebook she now carried, and then, honestly, wrote underneath it: but maybe I just got lucky.

An epicure from the dining room, a regular with a linen jacket who always ordered the chocolate tart and always had something to say about it, came through the kitchen one evening to compliment the pastry and lingered at Morgan's station while she poured a test shell into a mold. She felt the old worry that he would find fault, that he would perform his palate for everyone. Instead he picked up a set shell from the counter, looked at its shine, broke off a corner, listened to the snap, ate it, and said nothing at all for a moment. "That," he said finally, "is the thing itself," and left, and Morgan decided that was the highest compliment the kitchen had given her, higher even than Ms. Li's occasional nod.

The last Saturday of the spring, she tempered a full batch alone, the double boiler at a careful distance, a towel folded under the bowl's far rim to catch any drip that might think about falling. The chocolate moved like something deciding to cooperate. She poured the shells, tapped out the bubbles, and set the molds on the rack, and then she and Harris and Zachariah stood around them while the chocolate set in the cool room, none of them saying much, all of them watching. When it had set, Morgan turned a shell out onto the counter, held it up to the light, and broke it in half. It snapped. Zachariah reached over and took the bigger piece.

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: Edward Elgar's Pomp and Circumstance March No. 1, the usual North American graduation processional, premiered in 1901 in Liverpool.
story:
The folding chairs had been set out on the football field in rows so straight they looked mathematical, and Jason stood at the end of the line of graduates with his gown bunched at the elbows because it was sized for someone broader. Behind him, Barrett was humming. It took Jason a moment to recognize the tune, and then he could not stop hearing it, the slow rising phrase that every school in North America seemed contractually obligated to play while seniors walked.

"Do you know where that's from?" Jason asked. "Like actually from."

Barrett kept humming for two bars, finishing the phrase with exaggerated dignity. "From graduations," he said. "It's from graduations, dude."

Jason pulled out his phone, shielding it against his gown so the monitors wouldn't see. The search came back instantly, and he read it twice to make sure he had it right. "It's by Elgar. Edward Elgar. Pomp and Circumstance, March Number One. It premiered in 1901, in Liverpool." He said it quietly, almost to himself, because something about the date pleased him. Everyone in the line had been born in the shadow of the internet, and yet they were about to process to a piece of music older than anyone's grandmother, older than the field they stood on, probably older than the school.

"Absolutely enunciate that next part," Barrett said, leaning over his shoulder. "Liverpool. Say it like a documentary."

"Liverpool," Jason said, and a girl two rows ahead, Megane, turned around and shushed them both, though her mouth was twitching.

The line began to move. The music swelled from speakers mounted on the goalposts, the real recording now, strings and brass, and Jason found his mind doing the strange double exposure it had been doing all month. Here he was in June, in a rented gown, and there he was in September, in a dorm three states away, and the two versions kept overlapping like transparencies on a lightbox. In March he had turned down the scholarship at the state school to go to the expensive one, and his father had said fine in a voice that was not fine, and Jason had spent three months not deciding whether he regretted it. Regret, he had learned in calculus, required knowing the counterfactual, and you never got to see the counterfactual. Mr. Das had told them that once, in the spring, about a lemma they'd been struggling with: you can prove a thing is true, he'd said, without ever knowing why it's true, and you have to make your peace with that or you'll never finish the proof.

Mr. Das was on the stage now, in a gray suit, shaking hands with each graduate after the principal read the name. Jason watched him. In sophomore year Jason had been convinced Mr. Das disliked him, had failed a quiz on purpose as a kind of test of it, an act of small self-destruction that still embarrassed him when he let himself remember it. Mr. Das had pulled him aside the next day and said only, "You are not destitute of ability. So why are you acting like you are?" Jason had never fully answered the question.

The names began. The sun sat heavy on everyone's shoulders, and the speakers crackled with each syllable. Megane walked before him, and Barrett, who removed his cap at the top of the steps like a man greeting royalty, to scattered laughter. Then Jason heard his own name, flattened by the principal's hurried pronunciation, and he crossed the stage, and it was Mr. Das's hand that took his.

"Mr. Das," Jason said. "That piece. The Elgar. Did you know it premiered in 1901, in Liverpool?"

Mr. Das's eyebrows went up, and for a second Jason thought he had made a fool of himself, holding up the line with trivia. Then Mr. Das said, "Liverpool. Yes." He handed over the diploma tube. "And you looked it up just now, in line, didn't you."

"How could you tell?"

"Because that is what you do," Mr. Das said. "You pull the thread before you walk through the door." The principal's voice was already calling the next name. Mr. Das leaned in, half a breath. "The one you wanted to pull and didn't, in March. Come by in August, before you leave. I'll be in the room."

Jason stepped off the far side of the stage with the tube in both hands, the marching music still rolling behind him, and sat down in his assigned chair without feeling the walk between them. Barrett was grinning at him from the next row. Jason held up the tube and turned it over once, and inside, instead of the diploma, he found a single folded sheet: his failed sophomore quiz, the one he'd blown on purpose, with a grade marked out and rewritten in red at the top, and beneath it, in Mr. Das's cramped hand, the words, proof deferred.

"Yo, you good?" Barrett said.

"Yeah," Jason said, folding the sheet closed again. "You coming in August?"

"August where?"

"Mr. Das's room," Jason said, and looked back toward the stage.

activity: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
knowledge_domain: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
fact: A naive narrator, such as Huck in Mark Twain's Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, reports events honestly but misunderstands them, so readers see more than the narrator does.
story:
Kaitlyn had built the reading nook herself out of a corner her mother had given up on, two cushions, a lamp with a broken shade tilted like a hat, and a shelf that held more tea mugs than books. She sat cross-legged in it on Saturday afternoon with Huckleberry Finn open on her knee, a sticky note on her forehead that said DO NOT TALK TO ME, which her brother had written on himself and then abandoned. The essay prompt from Mr. Kim sat beside her: is the narrator telling you the truth, and does it matter?

Maina arrived at three, let herself in as usual, and peeled the sticky note off Kaitlyn's forehead to read it. "You wrote this to yourself," she said. "That's a new level of bossy."

"Braylon wrote it. He's punishing me for last weekend." Kaitlyn held up the book. "Anyway, sit. I need your brain."

"My brain charges by the hour." Maina folded herself into the other cushion and stole a mug of cold tea, grimaced, and drank it anyway.

"Here's the thing." Kaitlyn flipped to a page she'd dog-eared, which Mr. Kim had told them was a crime. "Huck keeps saying these things, and I laughed out loud on the bus, and then I got embarrassed, and then I got confused. Because the joke is on him, right? He reports everything so honestly, and then he gets it wrong. It's like watching someone describe a magic trick while it's happening to them."

Maina took the book and read the page, lips moving slightly, which she would deny. "Okay, wait. He's describing the whole thing and he still doesn't see it."

"Right. So I trust him and I don't trust him at the same time. That's the part I can't get into the essay." Kaitlyn pulled her notebook over and found the paragraph she'd abandoned, which ended mid-sentence with the word "however" and then a small drawing of a fish. "Mr. Kim keeps saying point of view shapes trust, but every time I try to write it, it turns into a book report."

Braylon came through the door without knocking, holding a bag of chips and his biology folder, which he dropped on the rug. "I brought montane flashcards," he announced. "Birds that live on mountains. Want to quiz me while you do your literature thing?"

"No," said Kaitlyn, and then, "Fine, but only the ones with funny names."

Maina read aloud: "Huck says he felt bad about helping Jim, and then he says he'd have felt bad if he hadn't." She looked up. "He means it. He's not lying at all. He just has it completely backwards, and Twain knows it, and we know it, and Huck doesn't."

Kaitlyn sat very still for a second, the way she did when a math problem turned over in her head and showed its underside. "That's it. He reports honestly and misunderstands, and we see more than he does. There's a name for that, I heard someone say it in class." She scrolled through her notes on her phone. "Naive narrator. That's the exact phrase. Huck is a naive narrator." She wrote it down and underlined it twice, then once more for luck.

"So your whole essay is just that?" Braylon held up a flashcard with a picture of a bird that looked offended. "One sentence, done, weekend free?"

"One sentence, and then everything funny in the book makes sense, is the thing." Kaitlyn counted on her fingers. "The scenes where I laughed on the bus. They're funny because Huck doesn't get the joke. He's the only one who doesn't." She paused. "Although. Now I have the opposite problem. If I say every funny scene works that way, that's too tidy. There's the part where Huck is genuinely clever, conning the slave hunters. I don't know where that goes."

"Put it in a paragraph that starts with however," said Maina, pointing at the dead sentence on the page.

"Everyone says however," said Kaitlyn, but she was already writing. Braylon quizzed himself on montane birds in the background, getting the chickadee wrong twice, and offered reparations for the sticky note in the form of chips, which Kaitlyn accepted with dignity. She wrote until her hand cramped, then read the paragraph out loud. It said that Huck tells the truth and misses it, that the reader stands in the gap, and that she still wasn't sure what to do about the parts where he was sharper than everyone around him. She left the uncertainty in. It looked strange on the page, like admitting a limp, but it also looked like hers.

Maina read it over her shoulder and nodded slowly. "Mr. Kim's going to circle that last part and write a question mark."

"Let him," said Kaitlyn. "I'll bring chips to class."

Braylon held up the final flashcard. "Last one. Mountain bird, very smug, starts with C."

"Condor," said Maina.

"Grouse," said Kaitlyn.

Braylon turned the card around and they both leaned in to look.

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: In a car with anti-lock brakes, a driver in an emergency should press the brake firmly and hold it rather than pump it, and can still steer.
story:
Grayson's grandfather had driven him to the empty church parking lot every Sunday that August, and every Sunday he had said the same thing: if you ever have to stop fast, pump the brakes. Tap and release, tap and release, like the pedal is a hot stove. His grandfather had learned it in 1974 from a man who had learned it from a driving instructor in Lachine, and it had become, in the family, something between advice and scripture. Grayson had nodded each time, his hands at ten and two, the station wagon crawling between faded yellow lines. So when his mother booked him a real lesson, with a real instructor, on real streets, he assumed it would be mostly a formality.

The instructor, Ms. Mensah, had him adjust the mirror before they left the driveway, which nobody in his family had ever done while the car was still parked. She rode in the passenger seat with her own brake pedal, which Grayson tried not to look at. In the back seat, Marius and Marc-Olivier sat with a bag of chips they had been told twice to close, because Marius had insisted on coming, and Marc-Olivier had insisted on coming wherever Marius went. "First road lesson," Marc-Olivier announced, as though commentating. "He's either going to stall it or hit a mailbox." "It's an automatic, genius," Marius said.

They drove out along the service road, past the dollar store and the shuttered video rental, and Grayson kept the car at exactly the speed limit, which felt to him like a moral position. Ms. Mensah had a way of speaking that reminded him of a debate coach he'd once had, someone who treated every question as though it had two respectable sides. When he admitted this, that he drove slowly out of principle, she said, "Principles are fine until a truck is behind you and a child is ahead of you, and then you find out which principle you actually hold." Marc-Olivier made a low ooooh sound from the back. Grayson did not answer, but he filed the sentence somewhere, the way he filed things.

It was near the intersection by the bakery that the cyclist came off the sidewalk. She wasn't supposed to be there, and she clearly knew it halfway through, and she froze in the middle of the right lane, wobbling, close enough that Grayson could see the strap of her helmet cutting into her chin. His grandfather's voice arrived before his own thoughts did. Tap and release, tap and release. His foot started to do exactly that, the car lurching, still travelling, the cyclist's front wheel tilted toward them, and Ms. Mensah said, calmly, in the tone of a person asking for the salt, "Hold it down. Firm. You can still steer." He pressed the pedal all the way and held it, and turned the wheel, and the car stopped in a hard, shuddering line that ended three metres short of her. She rode off without looking at them, which felt, strangely, like the worst part.

They pulled into the plaza and sat with the engine running. Grayson's hands were trembling on the wheel and he kept them there so no one would see. "Your grandfather taught you to pump," Ms. Mensah said, not as a question. "How did you know that?" "Because you were doing it beautifully, and it's wrong for this car." He told her about the Sundays, the parking lot, 1974, the man from Lachine. Marius leaned forward between the seats. "Wait, so Grandpa's advice is just obsolete?" "It's not obsolete," Grayson heard himself say, surprising himself. "It's right for cars without anti-lock brakes. This car has them, so it's wrong here." He had read the word somewhere, he realised, in the manual, at midnight, and understood it only now, with the shudder still in his foot.

He thought about how easily he could have dismissed his grandfather entirely, could have gone home and said the old man didn't know anything, made a joke of it with Marius and Marc-Olivier in the group chat. Plenty of people did exactly that, filed every older opinion under a single heading and stigmatized the whole generation as out of touch. His grandfather was not a dilettante about cars; he had rebuilt an engine on the garage floor when Grayson was eight. What his grandfather had been, Grayson decided, was a man who had stopped updating, not because he was foolish but because for most of his life there had been nothing to update. Whether that made him less sagacious, or more, was not something Grayson could settle in the front seat of a Corolla.

"That was good recovery," Ms. Mensah said, pulling out her clipboard. "When you brake like that and hold it, you can still steer around something instead of just stopping. That's the whole point." She marked something, and Marc-Olivier reached over the seat to try to see the grade, and Marius slapped his hand away. "I don't want a grade," Grayson said. "I want to know what I'd have done if you hadn't been sitting there." "Nobody gets to know that," she said, putting the clipboard down. "You'd have done something, and you'd live with it, same as everyone."

On the drive home she let him take the long way, past his grandfather's street. He slowed at the corner without being told, checked the mirrors the way she had shown him, and tried to imagine the Sunday conversation that was coming, how he would explain it without making it sound like a correction. Maybe he'd just ask to see the old car, the one without the anti-lock brakes, and let his grandfather be the expert one more time. Ms. Mensah's phone buzzed and she silenced it. At the stop sign he pressed the brake once, firmly, and held it until the car was still.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The yellow first-down line shown on televised American football is computer-drawn; it was first broadcast on ESPN on September 27, 1998, by a company called Sportvision.
story:
The living room had reached its Sunday density: her father in the recliner, Anissa and Everett crammed onto the couch with bowls balanced on their knees, and Amy's little cousin Marco sprawled on the rug with his chin propped on his fists, six years old and certain about everything. On the screen the quarterback barked signals, and Marco pointed at the television with the authority of a customs official.

"That yellow line is painted on the grass," he announced. "They paint it before every play and then they scrub it off really fast."

Amy set down her drink. "Marco, they can't paint it between plays. The guys are standing right there." She waved at the screen, where a linebacker was, at that moment, standing on the line in question, his cleats plainly visible through the yellow stripe. Marco frowned at this evidence the way people frown at weather.

"Then it's paint that doesn't cover shoes," he said, which was, Amy had to admit, a theory of sorts. Everett leaned forward, delighted. "It's magic paint," he offered. "Paint from a wizard." Marco considered this seriously, which was the problem with Everett: he could never tell which of his own jokes were jokes.

"Everett, you're being deleterious to his education," Anissa said, throwing a popcorn kernel at him. "That's a real word, Amy, tell him."

"It's real," Amy said, though she was already reaching for her phone, because the truth was she didn't know either. She had watched football her whole life and had never once asked where the line came from. It was simply there, like the score in the corner, like the grass itself. She typed it out: how does the tv football yellow line work.

The answer made her laugh out loud, which made Marco sit up, indignant, assuming he was being laughed at. "It's not paint at all," she said. "It's drawn on by a computer, over the picture. A company called Sportvision did it first, and it showed up on ESPN on September 27, 1998." She turned the phone toward Marco, then thought better of it, since he read at the level of restaurant menus. "So it's not on the field. It's only on your TV."

Marco absorbed this with visible struggle, the way a scale resettles when a weight slides to the other side. "So the players can't see it?"

"Nobody on the field can see it," Amy said. "Only us."

"Then how do they know where to go?"

Amy opened her mouth and closed it. That was the twist, the small one anyway: the line she had always trusted as a guide was invisible to the people it appeared to measure. The players found their way by chains and stakes and orange markers, the old clumsy instruments, while the clean yellow line existed solely for the couch. She said as much, and Anissa nodded slowly. "It's like rationalism," Anissa said, who had just finished a philosophy unit and was deploying it everywhere. "The pretty perfect version that only exists in your head, versus the messy real thing on the ground."

"That is not what that word means," Everett said.

"It's close to what it means," Anissa said.

Marco, meanwhile, had changed his mind entirely, which he did the way thunderstorms happen, all at once and with commitment. "The computer line is better," he declared. "Paint would get the players' shoes yellow." He pointed at the screen again, vindicated, as the running back stretched the ball past the electronic stripe and the crowd roared. First down. Marco looked around the living room to make sure everyone had seen him be right about the outcome, if not the method.

Amy's father, who had been silent through all of it in the manner of a man conserving attention for the game, finally spoke from the recliner. "You know who paid for that line, back at the start? Networks did. Advertising money underwrites the whole thing. The yellow line, the cameras, the wizard paint, all of it." He took a sip of his drink, pleased with himself.

Amy sat back between her friends and watched the drive continue, third down, then a timeout, then the crowd noise swelling for no reason she could determine. She still wasn't sure which version of the line she preferred: the one in the room with them, bright and confident and only for the audience, or the invisible rules the players actually used. Marco had already moved on and was narrating the game to nobody, providing the players with advice they could not hear. The yellow line glowed on, steady and helpful and entirely unbothered.

"Throw it to the fast guy!" Marco shouted at the screen.

"Which one's the fast guy?" Everett asked.

"All of them," Marco said. "They're all faster than you."

activity: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
knowledge_domain: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
fact: In countries where tax is withheld from pay, such as the US and Canada, a tax refund means more was withheld during the year than was owed; it is an overpayment returned, not extra income.
story:
I already knew about taxes before the unit started, which is what I kept telling Ryley, though if I am being accurate, what I knew came mostly from listening to my mother on the phone with her sister in April, both of them saying words like "return" and "refund" in the tone people reserve for lottery numbers. Ms. Popal's business classroom smelled like dry-erase marker and the custodian's lemon cleaner, and on the first morning of the unit she taped a photocopied paycheque to the whiteboard, blown up so large the numbers looked like accusations. I sat beside Ryley, who had a biology textbook open under the desk because he was failing that class the way rivers fail to stay inside their banks, and above his phylogeny diagrams of finches and their shared ancestors, Ms. Popal was pointing at the long column of letters: CPP, EI, FIT.

"Nobody take out phones," she said. "I want you to actually read this." She tapped the gross pay line and then the net pay line, and the gap between them, item by item, was the lesson. Deductions, she called them, before tax was even owed, taken off every pay period. I wrote nothing down because I intended to remember it all, and later, when I could not, I would claim I had.

The concrete part, the part that actually happened, came that Friday. Courtney burst in before the bell with her banking app held up like a trophy, announcing that her brother's refund had landed, four hundred dollars, and that he was taking everyone to the drive-thru. "Free money," she said, dropping into her seat. "The government just gives it to you in the spring."

"Every year?" Ryley asked, already planning his own spring.

I opened my mouth and then closed it, because something in my mother's April phone calls rearranged itself in my head. Her refund arriving in a year when her hours at the store had been cut, and her saying to my aunt, "They took too much off my cheques, that's all it is." I had thought she was being modest. Now, in Ms. Popal's classroom, with the enlarged paycheque still faintly visible under half-erased marker, I understood her differently. The deductions I had copied down, or half copied, were the whole story of where a refund came from.

"It's not extra," I said. Courtney turned around. "It's not free money. It's an overpayment. They take the tax off your pay all year, and if more was withheld than you owed, they give the overpayment back." The words came out flatter than I wanted, like I was reading them off a receipt. Courtney said her brother would be devastated to learn he had only loaned the government his own money interest-free, and Ryley laughed, and then, quieter, said, "Wait, so my mom's refund is just her own paycheque coming back late?" I said I thought so, and I did think so, and I also noted, privately, that I had spent three Aprils believing the same thing Courtney believed, which I decided not to mention.

That weekend I did the receipts. My mother keeps every one in a shoebox, and I sat at the kitchen table adding up the sales tax on groceries that were taxed and groceries that were not, on the bus pass, on the winter boots from October. Thirteen percent on some things, nothing on others, the rules winding through the till like the river behind our old apartment wound through its riparian strip of willows, visible from only certain windows. At the bottom of the shoebox was her return from last year, folded into a square, and I unfolded it on the table and ran my finger down lines I did not fully understand, lines that adjusted and credited and subtracted, until I reached the number and recognized it as the one she had described to my aunt as her little windfall. Her own wages, portioned out across fourteen paycheques, returned in one lump that felt like a gift because of when it came.

On Monday, Ms. Popal had us calculate a sample refund from a fictional worker's figures, and Courtney, still grumbling, got it right on the first try, which surprised me enough that I excoriated myself silently for having assumed she would not. She had looked at the withheld column, looked at the owed column, and seen the difference plain as arithmetic. Ryley leaned over from the next row, his phylogeny homework now folded into a paper airplane he was too distracted to fly, and asked whether it was better to get a big refund or a small one. I said I didn't know. I said you could argue a big refund meant you'd lent your money away all year, and you could argue the opposite, that the little lump in spring had paid for our boots and our bus passes, and that a number is not the same thing as what a number does to a person's April.

I took the shoebox back to my mother's room that evening and put it where it belonged, under the bed, and she asked from the doorway what I had been doing with it. I started to explain, the overpayment, the withholding, the whole tidy mechanism I had assembled, and she listened with her coat still on, keys in hand, night shift ahead of her.

"Windfall," she said, and smiled, and went to find her shoes.

activity: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
knowledge_domain: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
fact: The European Union's AI Act, which entered into force on August 1, 2024, bans some uses of AI outright, including social scoring of people.
story:
The email arrived on a Thursday, from an address Vincent didn't recognize, with a subject line that read simply "Student Engagement Report." He opened it at his desk with a slice of pizza cooling on a napkin beside the keyboard, and found a dashboard: his name, his student ID, and a number, 82, beside a small colored bar trending green. The software, something called Coursewise, had apparently been watching him all semester. It logged his logins, his minutes on the school portal, the timestamps of his document drafts, even the intervals between his posts in the class forum. At the bottom, in smaller type, it said the score factored "behavioral engagement patterns" and would be shared with his college counselor.

He called Jayda first, because Jayda understood systems the way other people understood weather. "Did you get one?" he asked. She had. Her score was 61, and the bar beside it was yellow. "I work nights now," she said, her voice flat over the speaker. "I do my homework at two in the morning in long bursts instead of little sips every day. The machine thinks that means I'm disengaged." She read him a line from her report, something about inconsistent participation suggesting low academic investment, and he could hear her flipping the page. "My grades are fine, Vincent. My grades are better than yours."

That stung, mostly because it was true, and it sat with him while he stared at his own green bar. His score was good because he was on the portal constantly, not because he was learning more. He'd spent half of October refreshing the soccer schedule page during study hall. Coursewise had counted every refresh as engagement. The software didn't know what he was doing, only when and how often, and it had mistaken his restlessness for diligence while mistaking Jayda's night shifts for apathy. He opened a chat window and typed to Joaquin, whose older brother lived in Lisbon. Joaquin's brother had sent him articles about European tech law, and Joaquin had developed opinions about them the way other people developed opinions about referees.

"That's social scoring," Joaquin typed back, almost immediately. "Ranking people by their behavior. My brother says the European Union banned it. There's this thing called the AI Act, went into force on the first of August, 2024. It bans some uses of AI outright, and social scoring of people is one of them. Over there, a school doing this to you would be illegal." Vincent read the message twice, then pasted the link into a search to check it, because Joaquin also believed, with total confidence, several things about chemtrails. But the law was real. The AI Act, in force since August 1, 2024, prohibited certain uses of AI entirely, and social scoring was on the list of what was banned. He sat back in his chair, pizza forgotten, and felt something shift in his understanding. It wasn't that no one could make this software. It was that somewhere, people had decided nobody should.

He wrote to Mr. Villanueva, his old civics teacher, who had once tried to inculcate in them the habit of asking who benefits whenever a rule exists. Vincent kept the email short: the report, the score, the question of whether anyone at the school had voted to adopt Coursewise, and a link about the AI Act. He didn't mention Jayda's 61. Then he called her back. "Would you appeal it?" he asked. "There's supposed to be a process. Ask for clemency from the machine." She laughed, a short, sullen sound, nothing like her usual laugh. "The machine doesn't grant clemency, Vincent. It doesn't even know it was wrong. That's the whole point. Nobody's wrong. There's just a number."

Mr. Villanueva replied the next morning, before Vincent had even brushed his teeth. He thanked Vincent for the link, said he hadn't known about the law, and confirmed that no one had voted, that Coursewise had come bundled with the district's new learning platform, switched on by an IT administrator two counties away. He also said something Vincent kept rereading: that the school could choose to follow the European standard even though no law here required it, and that a student bringing the question to a school board meeting would be doing exactly the kind of thing his class had talked about all year. Then, at the bottom, a caveat. The software also flagged students who might be struggling, the ones whose activity dropped off sharply, and the counselor had used those flags to reach two kids last spring who hadn't been answering their emails. The system saw things teachers missed. That was true too.

On Saturday, Vincent and Jayda sat in his kitchen with the laptop between them, drafting an email to the school board. Jayda typed faster, so she drove while he argued for softer language, then against softening it, then for a paragraph that admitted the early-warning flags had done some good. She paused over that one, fingers hovering. "You want to tell them the thing that hurts our case?" "I want them to know we know," he said. "Otherwise we're just doing what the machine does, only picking the numbers we like." She looked at him for a long moment, then kept the paragraph.

They sent it that evening. No one had answered by Monday, and Mr. Villanueva warned him these things moved slowly, if they moved at all. Vincent still didn't know whether the school would turn the software off, keep it, or bury the question in committee until everyone graduated. What he knew was smaller and harder to hold: that the same system could flag a drowning kid and sink a tired one, that Europe had drawn a line his country hadn't, and that Jayda's yellow bar still glowed in a dashboard somewhere, updating itself regardless of anything they'd written. He opened his portal to check for a reply, watched his own minutes tick upward in real time, and closed the laptop lid.

activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
knowledge_domain: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
fact: The Taylor rule, proposed by economist John Taylor, says that when inflation rises one percentage point a central bank should raise its interest rate by more than one percentage point.
story:
Carson restocked the shelf of canned tomatoes for the third time that afternoon, not because anyone had bought them but because the boxes in the back needed clearing and the tomatoes were the lightest thing in the load. He worked Saturdays and two evenings a week at Okafor's Market, a narrow grocery wedged between a laundromat and a defunct travel agency, and he had learned in three months that the job was mostly a series of small contrivances for making time pass: rotating the milk, wiping the cooler doors, straightening labels so every can faced forward like a soldier at inspection. Between tasks he kept a folded sheet of paper in his apron pocket, covered in notes from Thursday's economics club meeting, and he took it out now and flattened it against the register counter.

At Thursday's meeting Jaiden had leaned back in his chair, pugnacious in the way he got when he thought he'd found a flaw in something official, and said that the whole interest rate business was simpler than the textbook made it. If inflation goes up one percentage point, he'd said, the central bank raises its rate one percentage point. You match it. Anything more is just the bank showing off. Their teacher had been called out of the room by then, a delivery arriving early, and the argument had migrated to the parking lot without anyone settling it.

Leo had followed Carson to his car. "You know it's not one for one," he'd said, hands in his pockets. "There's a thing called the Taylor rule. John Taylor, the economist. When inflation rises one percentage point, the central bank should raise its interest rate by more than that. More than one percentage point." Carson had asked why, and Leo had shrugged and said he didn't remember the why, only the rule, which had struck Carson as a strange way to know something.

Now, on the quiet Saturday, he laid the paper on the counter and tried to build the why himself, because he didn't like carrying a rule around without its reasons. He had written two questions in the margin. What does the bank control, exactly? And what does it want? The store around him seemed to adumbrate an answer without giving it: the prices taped to the shelves, the small note by the register about the bread going up another thirty cents, the older woman who had put back the good olive oil and taken the store brand. The whole market was a slow argument about what things cost and what people would pay.

Mr. Watanabe came in at four, as he always did, in his canvas jacket, and bought the same bag of rice, the same green tea, a single lemon. He was a neighbour of Carson's parents and had retired from something no one had specified, and he read two newspapers a day, and Carson liked him because he asked real questions and then waited for real answers. Today he glanced at the paper on the counter, its columns and arrows, and raised an eyebrow.

"Economics club," Carson said. "We got into a fight about interest rates. Jaiden thinks the central bank just matches inflation when it rises. Leo says no, you have to go further. There's a rule about it."

"Which do you believe?"

"That's the thing. I believed Jaiden on Thursday because his version is cleaner. Then Leo said the rule and I believed him because it had a name, which isn't actually a reason." He turned the paper over, where he had tried to sketch it. "I think the truth is somewhere in what the rule is for, not just what it says. If the bank only matches, then money stays just as cheap as it was, more or less, and cheap money is how prices got moving in the first place. Going further is how the bank makes its point stick." He heard himself say it and checked it against the rule in his head. One point of inflation, more than one point of rate. The direction held. He still couldn't say how much more, or when, or whether the bank ever got it wrong, and he said so.

Mr. Watanabe paid for his lemon and tea and rice, counted his change, and slid it into his jacket pocket. "You've changed your mind twice in two days and you're honest about the part you don't know," he said. "That's better than most people manage in a decade."

Carson refolded the paper and put it back in his apron. On Monday he would find Jaiden before first period, not to beat him, but because he wanted to hear the counterargument, now that he had something worth countering. He picked up the cloth, sprayed the cooler glass, and wiped it in long even strokes until the rows of milk showed through, bright and upright in the cold.

activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
knowledge_domain: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
fact: The '10 percent rule', never raising weekly running distance more than 10 percent, is a popular guideline, but studies have not shown it prevents injuries better than other gradual plans.
story:
Leo had filled the last page of his notebook before the first week of pre-season even ended, and now he sat on the bottom row of the bleachers at the track, transcribing the numbers onto a fresh sheet in neater handwriting. Mondays tempo runs, Wednesdays intervals, Fridays long runs, and a hard rule printed at the top and underlined twice: never add more than 10 percent to total weekly mileage. He had found it online in July and copied it the way he copied formulas before a physics exam, as if it were a law someone had proved.

Kasey dropped onto the bench beside him, sneakers still dusty from the warm-up laps. "What's all that?" She leaned over his shoulder before he could angle the notebook away.

"My season plan. Twelve weeks, building up to counties. It's called the 10 percent rule," Leo said, tapping the underlined line. "You never raise your weekly distance by more than 10 percent, so you don't get hurt."

Kasey pulled the notebook toward her, and he let her, because Kasey was the one who had run varsity as a sophomore and who wanted, openly and without apology, the anchor leg of the relay this spring. She studied the columns of numbers with the morose attention she gave anything that wasn't race day itself. "Where'd you get it?"

"Everywhere. It's like the rule. Every site says it."

"That's not the same as it being science," Kasey said, but she said it flatly, without conviction, and handed the notebook back.

It was Hafsa, stretching on the infield grass an hour later, who said the thing that undid him. Leo had been explaining his build-up, week by week, and she interrupted before he reached week eight. "My cousin did her thesis on this. The 10 percent rule, never raising weekly distance more than 10 percent. It's popular, but the studies haven't shown it prevents injuries any better than other gradual plans." She switched legs in her stretch. "Nobody proved it. It's just a guideline that got famous."

Leo stood there with his spikes in one hand, feeling the pages of his notebook turn, in his mind, from law into suggestion. "Then what am I supposed to do? Just guess?"

"Maybe plan something you can actually follow," Hafsa said. "With rest days you don't skip. And warm-ups you don't rush. That part nobody disputes."

He wanted to argue, and the wanting itself surprised him, because he had spent two years being the boy who coasted, who showed up late and jogged the cooldown, and this notebook was his proof of change. If the rule wasn't science, then his transformation wasn't disciplined; it was only decorated. He ran his intervals that afternoon with his heart not quite in it, and afterward, in the equipment shed, he found Mr. Kang rolling the hurdle mats. Leo asked him, testing, whether the 10 percent rule was true. Mr. Kang said only, "Where'd you hear that?" and went back to the mats, and Leo understood he would get nothing from that quarter either.

That night he sat at the kitchen table and started over, and the second plan looked less like a cathedral. He kept the gradual build, because going up slowly still made sense to him even unproven; he added two rest days instead of one; he wrote WARM-UP: FULL TEN MINUTES in the margin of every single session, since that was the part he had always cheated. But beside week six, where the old plan had a precise 10 percent jump calculated to the decimal, he left a blank box and wrote a question mark in it. Some weeks he felt strong, some weeks he didn't, and no rule he'd found could tell him which kind of week was coming. He was honest enough with himself to admit that the blank box scared him a little, and that it also freed him.

On Monday he showed the new plan to Kasey by the water station before practice, holding it against the wind. She looked at it for a long time, longer than the old one, and Leo realized she wasn't reading the mileage; she was looking at the relay weeks, the ones marked with the letters AK, her initials penciled faintly beside the speed sessions, as if she'd already claimed them. She had her own season drawn somewhere in her head, and his notebook was only where it crossed his.

"Ten-minute warm-ups," she said finally. "Every day. You'll actually do that?"

"I'm going to try."

"Then I'll check," Kasey said, and she took the stopwatch out of the equipment bag without asking, and started the clock.

activity: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
knowledge_domain: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
fact: During Chuseok, Korea's harvest festival on the 15th day of the eighth lunar month, many families hold charye, a memorial rite that sets out food for their ancestors.
story:
The note from his grandmother arrived on Tuesday, folded inside a manila envelope with two sheets of directions and a stick of dried persimmon. Parker read it standing at the mailbox while Michaela's text buzzed in his pocket. Her message said: you're seriously doing the whole thing? The whole table? and he typed back that he was, that Halmeoni had decided this fall it would be him, and that he had less than a week to learn what his father and uncles had absorbed over thirty years of watching. Then he went inside and spread the letter on the kitchen table, where the light through the blinds cut it into stripes.

The letter said what the letter had always said, in her careful print: Chuseok falls on the fifteenth day of the eighth lunar month, the harvest festival, and before the feast comes charye, a memorial rite that sets out food for the ancestors. His grandmother had written it out the way she wrote out recipes, quantities unstated, order assumed. Rice on the east, soup on the west, fruit at the ends farthest from the door, and beneath that a line he read four times: You will not remember where anything goes. That is not the point. The point is to ask.
