He had watched the rite every autumn of his life from the folding chairs near the garage, but watching, it turned out, was not the same as knowing. On Thursday he set up a practice run in the living room with a card table and his mother's good dishes, and he got it wrong immediately, put the soup where the rice belonged, and his father walked through on his way to the car and stopped with his coat still on. "Soup goes west," his father said, not unkindly, and Parker stood there feeling the strangeness of it, that a direction could be a fact, that east and west could matter more than whether the broth was salted.

He called Odin, who came over Friday with his skateboard under his arm and a genuinely useless amount of confidence. Odin's family was Nigerian and his own harvest instincts ran toward jollof rice and standing around a grill, so he mostly sat on the couch offering commentary while Parker rearranged the table for the fourth time. "This is like a chess board," Odin said. "Every dish has a square." Parker said it was more like a language where the grammar was geography, and Odin said that was the most Parker sentence he had ever heard, and then asked whether Parker actually believed the ancestors ate the food. Parker didn't answer right away. He moved the dried fish, then moved it back.

That was the question he kept circling all week, and he was honest with himself that he circled it rather than answering it. He had read, in some late-night spiral of searching, about how holidays get commodified, packaged into sales and seasonal lattes until the original shape of them is hard to find, and he understood that argument, even agreed with parts of it. But kneeling at the card table at midnight, moving a bowl of chestnuts two inches east, he felt the opposite problem too, which was that a ritual you don't practice at all doesn't stay pure. It just disappears. The food on the table was food; his father would eat the pears afterward; nobody thought otherwise. And still the arranging was not nothing. He couldn't have said what it was, exactly, and he was getting less comfortable pretending he could.

Michaela, who was staying in town for the weekend, texted him a photograph of her own family's long table at their parish hall, all mismatched platters, with the caption: is this anything like yours? He sent back a picture of the practice table, the turbid glass of persimmon punch he'd made from a recipe he'd misread, cloudy and too sweet, sitting at the wrong end entirely. She replied: yours looks like it means something. He looked at the photo for a while, deciding whether that was a compliment or a question.

Saturday morning he knocked on Mr. Mwangi's door with the persimmon stick as a peace offering, because Mr. Mwangi had lived next door since Parker was six and was the only adult Parker knew who would answer a question straight. Parker asked him whether he thought ceremonies for the dead were belief or habit. Mr. Mwangi accepted the persimmon, turned it over in his hands, and said, "You sound like a pedagogue already, and you're seventeen. Sit down." They sat on the porch. He said that in his village the ancestors were fed before the children, every feast, and nobody ever asked the question Parker had just asked, and that maybe the asking was its own kind of honoring, or maybe it was just noise, and that Parker would have to decide which, probably more than once. Then he ate the persimmon and said nothing else.

On the day itself, the whole family crowded into the garage bay where the long table stood under a canopy of plastic sheeting, cousins on coolers, an uncle filming vertically, his grandmother in the chair nearest the wall. Parker knelt at the table with the tray of fruit and stopped. East. Rice on the east. His mind went white, and then, out of the white, came the letter's line, and he turned and asked his grandmother, loudly enough that the filming uncle adjusted his phone, "Halmeoni, the chestnuts, which side?" She said, "East, with the fruit, far from the door," and he set them down, and his father, standing behind him, said nothing at all, which Parker was learning to read correctly.

The incense went up in a slow rope. The family bowed behind him, twice, his little cousin copying the angle of everyone else's spine. When it was over and the food began moving to the folding tables, his grandmother gripped his wrist and pulled him down to her chair. "Next year," she said, "you will not ask." Parker said, "Then I'll ask anyway," and went to carry in the soup.

activity: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
knowledge_domain: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
fact: In the United States, most negative information on a credit report, such as late payments, can be reported for seven years, and bankruptcies for up to ten.
story:
The open house had turned the engineering building into a marketplace, and Jake moved through it with the folded program going soft in his hands. Lohan walked beside him, holding a coffee he had bought with a new credit card, the first either of them had ever seen up close, matte black with his name printed small. Zavier was supposed to meet them at the session on residence halls, but he had texted that he was still arguing with his mother outside the library, so Jake and Lohan drifted toward a table where upper-year students in matching T-shirts were answering questions about money.

"I missed the payment on it," Lohan said, turning the card over in his fingers. "The first one. They sent me an email and I forgot again, and then they charged me a fee, whatever. It's forty dollars."

A girl at the table, maybe nineteen, with a lanyard that said STUDENT AMBASSADOR, looked up from her stack of pamphlets. "Do you mean you paid it late, or you still haven't paid it?"

"Late. Paid it like ten days late. My dad said forget it."

She set down the pamphlets. "Okay, so I work at the financial aid office part time, and I see this all day. Late payments can stay on your credit report for seven years." She said it plainly, the way someone says a bus route. "And if it ever got bad enough that you declared bankruptcy, that's up to ten. Seven and ten. That's the window. It follows you."

Lohan laughed, but the laugh came out thinner than he meant it to. "Seven years? For forty dollars?"

"Seven years," she said, and she didn't smile, which somehow made it land. "I'm not saying it ruins you. I'm saying when you're twenty-five and you're applying for a lease, it's still in the file."

Jake watched Lohan's face do something complicated. Lohan was the blase one, the one who had shrugged off the deferred acceptance, the parking ticket, the girl in calculus, and Jake had always envied the shrug, the way it let Lohan move unburdened through rooms Jake left carrying everything. But now Lohan slid the card back into his wallet slowly, like it had changed weight.

"Zavier's the one who should hear this," Jake said. "He wants to sign a lease in the fall." That was Zavier's whole plan, laid out on the drive here: apartment instead of residence, because residence was for kids, because Zavier wanted a door he could close on his mother's opinions. She wanted him in residence, safe and fed and accounted for, and the argument outside the library was the same argument from March and April.

They found him on a bench under the broad steps, phone dark in his lap, looking less like someone who had lost than someone still deciding what losing meant. Jake sat down and told him what the ambassador had said, the numbers exactly, seven and ten, and Zavier listened with his chin on his fist.

"So a landlord pulls that file," Zavier said. "And my name's attached to stuff from when I was eighteen."

"From before eighteen," Lohan said. "Which is the insane part. You sign things before you know what a file even is."

The session on residence halls was starting, and a woman from the university, Ms. Farah-Ali, was at the door checking people in, greeting each student by the name on their tag and asking, genuinely, whether they'd found the coffee yet. When Jake reached her she read his tag and said, "Jake, good, come in, we saved seats at the front," and it was such a small thing, the saving of seats, but he felt it all the way to his sternum. He stopped in the doorway instead of going in.

"Can I ask you something that isn't about residence?" he said. "If a landlord asks someone to co-sign, to indemnify them if I don't pay, is that normal? Is that a bad sign?"

Ms. Farah-Ali considered it. "It's common. It means somebody else's file answers for yours." She glanced toward the bench where Zavier sat. "For some students it's the only way the lease happens. Whether it's a bad sign depends on who's standing behind you." She held the door. "You can come in late, the seats will hold."

Jake stayed outside. He sat down next to Zavier, who was now looking at the residence photos on his phone, brick and ivy and a dining hall with long tables, and Jake understood that what he was watching was not a decision being made but a decision being approached, slowly, from a long way off.

"If you take the apartment," Jake said carefully, "and your mom co-signs, she's not just giving in. She's the one carrying it if you mess up. That's what indemnify means. She'd be the surety. You'd be the, I don't know, the person it's all for."

"My mom called it a fiduciary thing," Zavier said. "She said a co-signer has a fiduciary duty, like she's managing something of mine and hers at the same time. She looked it up in the car. She had a whole speech." He turned the phone off. "I tuned most of it out, but I remember that word."

Lohan came back out with a stolen cookie from the refreshment table, two actually, and handed one each to Jake and Zavier without being asked, which was Lohan's way of apologizing for every shrug he'd ever performed. They sat on the bench eating, and the campus went on around them, tour groups rotating through the quad like weather.

"I set up autopay," Lohan said, crumbs on his shirt. "Just now, on the app. Took ninety seconds." He said it with faint wonder, as if he had discovered that the future could be handled in increments, on a phone, between cookies.

Zavier stood and pocketed his phone. "I'm going to go find my mom," he said. "Not to agree to anything. Just to hear the rest of the speech."

He went up the wide steps two at a time, and Jake watched him until the crowd took him.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Mise en place is a French cooking term meaning 'putting in place': measuring and preparing all the ingredients before starting to cook.
story:
The recipe lay flat on the counter where her grandmother had left it, held open by a jar of paprika, and Keira read it twice before touching anything. Her grandmother was still in the hospital, three days now, and the house smelled like cold dish soap and the ghost of Sunday roasts. The plan had been simple: make the lemon cake exactly as the recipe said, carry it to the fourth floor, and set it on the tray table beside the bed before visiting hours ended. Her grandfather had offered to help, but he stood at the doorway with his hands in his pockets, useless in his own kitchen, and she had told him to go find the good cake tin instead.

She creamed the butter and sugar until they paled, cracked in the vanilla, grated the lemon zest with more care than she had ever grated anything. The recipe was written in her grandmother's looping hand, with margins full of small notes. Add the flour slowly. Don't rush the eggs. Keira, if you're making this, read the next page before you begin. She had not read the next page. She had been too eager, too certain that a cake was a cake, and it was only when she reached the line that said fold in three beaten eggs that she opened the refrigerator and found the egg tray holding one egg, cracked along the top like a bad joke.

"Grandpa," she called, "do we have eggs anywhere? The fridge is basically empty."

He appeared in the doorway still holding the cake tin. "She does the shopping Saturdays. I eat what appears." He looked so apologetic that she softened, and she fished out her phone to message Cloe, who worked Saturdays at the grocery and would know whether the store could deliver in an hour. While she typed, her eye caught the margin note again. Read the next page before you begin. She turned the page with one buttery finger.

At the top, in pencil, her grandmother had written: Mise en place. French. It means putting in place, everything measured and ready before you start. Below it: I learned this the hard way in 1978, with a birthday cake and no eggs. Do not be like me at twenty-two.

Keira laughed out loud, alone in the kitchen, and then nearly cried, and then did neither and instead finished typing to Cloe: grandmother's recipe literally has mise en place written on it and I ignored it and now the batter is sitting here waiting on eggs. Can you get someone to run three over, or are you not allowed to leave?

The reply came in bursts. omg. okay so I can't leave the register until 4. BUT. mr gill lives two doors from your grandmother's, right? the one with the chickens?? he sells eggs to half the street, I bet. also my cousin says I should monetize a page where I just document other people's kitchen disasters, you'd be the pilot episode. Keira texted back that Cloe could monetize her funeral, and then she looked at her grandfather, who was still hovering, and gave him something to do.

"Go two doors down and ask Mr. Gill if we can buy three eggs. Tell him it's for her lemon cake and he'll say yes."

He went, moving faster than she'd seen him move all week, and while he was gone she covered the bowl with a tea towel and sat on the counter stool and read the whole recipe through, twice, front to back. The oven needed preheating; the tin needed greasing; the last instruction said cool in the pan for ten minutes only, or the bottom steams. She did all of it, in order, and understood that her grandmother hadn't been scolding her from the page. She'd been standing where Keira now stood, at twenty-two, batter waiting, and she had written it down so that somebody after her would not. It wasn't luck or happenstance that the note existed. It was the whole point of it, a hand reaching forward through the recipe.

Mr. Gill came back with her grandfather, carrying not three eggs but six in a folded paper bag, and refused the two dollars she found in the drawer by the stove. "She feeds my birds' table scraps all summer," he said. "There's a balance." He lingered in the doorway while she folded the beaten eggs into the batter, and when she offered him a slice if he came back tomorrow, he said he wasn't sanguine about hospital cake making it home untouched, but he'd take his chances.

The cake went in on the middle shelf, and Keira set the timer, and then wrote MISE EN PLACE on a sticky note and pressed it to the fridge at exactly her grandmother's eye level. Her grandfather saw her do it and cleared his throat and said nothing, and she went to get the good knife for the lemons still sitting in the bowl.

activity: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
knowledge_domain: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
fact: The United States has no national sales tax; sales taxes are set by states and local governments, so the rate on a receipt depends on where the purchase is made.
story:
The paycheque felt heavier than the paper it was printed on. Evan turned it over twice outside the bank, checking the numbers against the hours he remembered sweating through: forty-two hours of hauling carts and bagging groceries at two dollars above minimum wage, which should have meant a small fortune, and yet the line that read NET PAY was almost sixty dollars lighter than the line above it. Federal income tax, state income tax, something called FICA. He had heard Mr. Joseph, his supervisor at the store, describe these as deductions, the government's share taken off the top, and promised that some of it might come back in a refund when Evan filed his first tax return in the spring. That promise did not help him today. Louka wanted two hundred and forty dollars for the road-trip deposit by tonight, and the trip itself was eleven days away.

Inside, the bank smelled like heated air and carpet cleaner. Evan waited behind a woman counting envelopes and rehearsed what he would say. The teller, a young man with a lanyard, slid the cheque back through the slot after looking at it for a long moment and said that as a new account holder, part of the funds would be held for a few business days. "How many business days?" Evan asked, and the teller said three, possibly five. The trip deposit was due tomorrow night. Evan stood there with his hands flat on the counter, doing arithmetic that kept sliding sideways on him.

He texted Louka from the lobby, thumbs clumsy. "Bank holding most of it. Can I get until Friday?" The reply came as a photograph first: a receipt from a gas station in Milford, a bottle of juice and a bag of chips, the total circled in blue pen. Then words. "Fine till Friday. But look at this. Same snacks cost me almost a dollar less in Ashby this morning. Same chain, same everything." Evan frowned at the screen. He had passed through both towns; Ashby sat right beside Milford on the map, close enough that the radio stations overlapped.

He called Ivy, who had done a civics project on taxes and would not let anyone forget it. "That's sales tax," she said when he told her. "The United States has no national sales tax. States and local governments set their own rates, so the tax on a receipt depends on where you buy the thing." She was eating something; he could hear it. "Milford's just pricier, apparently. Or Ashby's cheaper. Someone decided, somewhere." She told him he should ask Louka which town had the lower rate, since they were stopping in one of them to fill the cooler, and then she had to go because her mother was calling her to adjudicate a dispute between her younger brothers over who had broken the blinds.

Evan sat in one of the molded chairs near the ATM and laid the paycheque stub and Louka's receipt side by side on his knee. Two documents, two kinds of tax. The stub showed money taken before it ever reached his hands, silently, in three separate lines; the receipt showed pennies and dimes added at a register, a different amount depending on which side of an invisible line you stood in. He had been thinking of taxes as one monolithic thing, an oligarchy of governments collecting tribute, but the evidence on his knee suggested something looser and stranger, a patchwork in which the very price of a bag of chips shifted between neighbouring towns.

The problem was still the two hundred and forty dollars. His mother could lend it, but she had been clear about the last loan and he did not want to ask twice. He went back to the teller's window and asked whether any portion cleared immediately. The teller said the first two hundred dollars of a deposited cheque was typically available the next business day, which would be tomorrow morning, forty dollars short of what Louka needed and one day ahead of the deadline only if Evan got up early.

He texted Louka again. "Two hundred tomorrow morning, forty on Friday from tips. Also stop in Ashby, not Milford, for the cooler stuff." Then he added, "I'll bring receipts." Louka replied with a thumbs-up and a picture of the deposit ledger he was keeping for the trip, a page of names and numbers already half filled, one entry crossed out because Nadia's boyfriend had become, in Louka's word, obstreperous at the party and lost his seat in the car.

Evan folded the paycheque stub into his wallet, keeping the receipt stub and Louka's photograph separate so he could show them to Ivy later, and walked out into the cold. At the corner he checked the time: 4:52, the bank closing behind him, eight minutes to catch the bus and twelve hours until the branch opened again. He ran for it, wallet slapping against his hip, and made the doors just as the driver reached for the lever.

activity: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
knowledge_domain: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
fact: The US Telecommunications Act of 1996 eliminated the national cap on radio station ownership, and the number of station owners then fell sharply even as the number of stations grew.
story:
Brody set his phone face down beside his plate the way his mother liked, then turned it over again almost immediately. On the screen was the message from Kiley, sent from her aunt's place in Phoenix: the same syndicated morning show she'd been hearing there was the one they both listened to in Columbus, same voices, same bits, same fake laugh at seven-forty. He'd told her that was impossible. She'd sent a photo of the station van.

"You're not eating," his father said, spooning rice onto his own plate.

"I'm eating." Brody picked up his fork. His mother asked about the college deposit, and he said the check was in the mail, which was true, and that the meal plan was sorted, which was not, and while they talked about the neighbor's fence he ate without tasting anything. Under the table his mind kept working at the problem like a tongue at a loose tooth. Two cities, six hundred miles apart, and the same three-hour block of radio filling both.

Later he cleared his plate and went out to the porch, where Ms. García was watering her mums in the last light. She had worked in radio once, in sales, and Brody had learned to ask her questions the way you panned a river, letting the turbid water run off and keeping whatever heavy thing stayed in the bottom of the pan. "Did stations used to be owned by, like, actual local people?" he asked.

"Everything's owned by somebody," Ms. García said. The hose hissed against the leaves. "The companies that own the most stations, they're not in the radio business. They're in the being-huge business." She clipped a dead bloom with her thumb and forefinger. "Used to be a company could only own so many stations in the whole country. Not anymore. Congress changed that in ninety-six."

"That's the year I was born," Brody said, and she laughed and said that made him practically part of the deregulation generation, which he had to look up on the porch steps, hunched over his phone. The Telecommunications Act of 1996. It had eliminated the national cap on radio station ownership. He sat with that for a moment. No cap meant somebody could own hundreds.

The numbers came from a paper he found through the library's site, a PDF with a graph like a pair of scissors opening. After the cap was gone, the number of station owners fell sharply, even as the number of stations kept growing. More stations, fewer owners. He read it twice, then a third time, because it seemed to contradict itself the way a funhouse mirror did, and then it didn't anymore. Kiley hadn't been noticing a coincidence in Phoenix. She'd been noticing the shape of the whole thing.

He was still on the steps when his father came out to take the trash down, and Brody said, without planning to, "Did you know one company can own a thousand radio stations?" His father said no, and then, after the trash can lid banged, "Who told you that?" And Brody, watching him stack the recycling with sudden care, understood that his father's company, the one with the logo on his fleece, the one that had flown him to Phoenix twice last year, was one of the advertisers whose money moved through those stations. Not a sycophant exactly. But a beneficiary, which might be the same thing wearing quieter shoes.

At the dinner table the next night his father brought it up himself, which Brody had not expected. "That radio thing you were on about," he said. "I asked around at work. It's true, more or less." He cut his chicken. "It's also how your aunt in Duluth gets any news at all up there. The big company kept the transmitter running after the local guy went bankrupt." His mother said that was a fair point, and his father said nothing, and the silence had edges on it.

Brody didn't answer right away. He was trying to hold both things without dropping either: the sameness of the voices in two cities, the deadening of that, and the transmitter in Duluth still humming because somebody far away had a reason to keep it on. He could cogitate on it all through senior year and not be sure which weighed more, and he decided, cutting his own chicken, that being unsure was going to have to be the position he defended. "I want to study it," he said. "Media, or policy, something like that." His father looked up. "In Phoenix they've got a whole school for it," Brody said. "Kiley sent me the link."

activity: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
knowledge_domain: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
fact: In England and Wales, a landlord must place a tenant's deposit in a government-backed protection scheme within 30 days of receiving it.
story:
The letter from the letting agency arrived on a Tuesday, and by Wednesday evening it had migrated from the counter to the kitchen table, where Jordyn's mother had pinned it under the fruit bowl as though it might otherwise escape. Jordyn sat across from it with her laptop open and her tea going cold, because Augustin had messaged her that afternoon: "question for you, money person," which was flattering and also a burden, since her qualifications amounted to having once balanced the household budget for a month when her mother worked doubles.

She called him. His face filled the screen in the flat light of a Leeds bedsit, and behind him she could see a radiator and half a poster he'd never finished unrolling. He'd signed the tenancy in June, he said, handed over five weeks of rent as a deposit, and received nothing since except a WhatsApp message saying "welcome aboard." No certificate, no email, no paperwork of any kind. "Is that normal?" he asked. "Everyone here says stop worrying. Lisa says landlords are just like that."

Jordyn did not know whether landlords were just like that. She knew what a deposit was in theory, money held against damage, and she knew it in practice, because the same fruit bowl had once sheltered a stack of documents for the flat they'd rented before her mother bought this one. That purchase she remembered more vividly: the years of saving toward a down payment while rent left each month and returned nothing, her mother saying the rent was the price of not owning, the mortgage the price of owning, and both prices paid in full and on time.

"Send me the date you paid," she told Augustin, and he did, and she started searching. It took her three tries to find the right phrasing and then the information arrived all at once, plainly stated on a government page, as facts sometimes do after hiding behind the wrong search terms. In England and Wales, a landlord must place a tenant's deposit in a government-backed protection scheme within 30 days of receiving it. She read it twice. Thirty days. Augustin's money had been sitting somewhere, or nowhere, for over two months.

"You're past thirty days," she said. "By a lot." On screen Augustin sat up, and behind him the unrolled half of the poster slid an inch down the wall and stopped. He asked what a protection scheme even was, and she said it was what it sounded like, a scheme, government-backed, that the money was supposed to be in, and that there should be paperwork proving it. She made him write down the phrase while she watched. He read it back to her like a diagnosis, and she said she wasn't a doctor, she was a girl at a kitchen table, which he seemed to find reassuring anyway.

While they talked, her mother came in and started excavating the refrigerator, a project with the character of an exhumation, items emerging one by one into the light and being assessed without sentiment. Jordyn relayed the situation in short form, and her mother snorted. She'd once had a landlord who'd kept a deposit for "professional cleaning" after four years of a tenancy, back before the schemes, and she described the man with an economy of contempt that made clear she could have gone on at length had she chosen to. She chose not to. She took her sandwich and left, and Jordyn understood that she had just been shown a piece of family epidemiology, the pattern of a disease and its history, transmitted not by lecture but by snort.

Augustin's flatmate wandered through the frame, loquacious after two beers, insisting that nothing would come of it, that landlords knew how to wait people out, that Augustin should just let it go until the end of the tenancy and then fight for the money back. Jordyn heard the appeal of that. Fighting later felt safer than writing now, and there was a version of her that agreed with him, the version that had watched her mother save for eleven years and learned that the safest relationship with money was a defensive crouch. But the crouch had a cost too, and she'd watched that as well: rent paid and gone, no deposit protected, nothing accumulating toward anything.

"I'm not saying sue anybody," she said. "I'm saying ask for the certificate in writing, today, and keep a copy of the message. They had thirty days. You're not being difficult by asking." Augustin said the flatmate was shaking his head somewhere offscreen. Jordyn said the flatmate didn't have six hundred pounds sitting in an envelope marked maybe. She still wasn't certain what would happen next, whether the landlord would produce paperwork in a week or nothing ever, whether the phrase she'd given him would open a door or just make a landlord dislike him. She was honest about that part too, because it seemed wrong to hand him certainty she didn't have.

Augustin said he'd write the email in the morning, when the flatmate was asleep, and then he tipped his head at the poster behind him, which had slid again and now hung from one corner like a flag of a country in dispute. "If I get the money back," he said, "I'm buying a proper frame for that thing."

"Buy the frame first," Jordyn said. "Then you'll have to get the money back."

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: The word diploma comes from a Greek word meaning "paper folded double," from the earlier practice of folding official documents.
story:
The parking lot smelled like hot asphalt and the carnations the mothers were wearing, and David stood between Emerik's truck and Alfred's rusted Civic with his gown unzipped to the waist because the June heat made the polyester feel like a garbage bag. His diploma folder was under his arm. He had carried it through the whole ceremony like a tray of food he wasn't allowed to eat yet.

"Open it," Emerik said, leaning against the truck bed. "I want to see if they actually put anything in there. My cousin says his was empty and they mailed the real one in July."

"That's a scam," Alfred said. He was still in his cap, tassel swinging, because Alfred refused to remove the cap until someone made him. He had a plan to wear it to the diner on Route 9 and had been trying to cajole the other two into matching for twenty minutes. "They can't hand you an empty folder. That's fraud."

David opened the folder flat across his palms. The paper inside was crisp, printed with his full name, David Antonio Reyes, which only his grandmother used, and it was not folded at all. He turned it over. Nothing on the back. He held it up to the light like a cashier checking a fifty.

"You know what diploma means?" he said. "I found out last week. Greek. Paper folded double. That's the whole word. They used to fold official documents in half, so the word for the fold became the word for the thing."

Emerik took his own folder out from behind the seat, where he'd tossed it, and examined the diploma with sudden scholarly interest. "Mine's not folded either. Not even a crease. They gave us unfolded paper folded double, technically. Somewhere a Greek is rolling over."

"Mr. Ho would love this," Alfred said. "Where's Mr. Ho?"

Mr. Ho was not hard to find; he taught Latin, which meant most students discovered him late and then felt robbed of three years, and a knot of them had surrounded his beige sedan near the flagpole. David watched him extract himself with the patience of a man used to being thanked in parking lots. He shook hands. He patted shoulders. When he reached the three of them, Alfred held up his cap in salute, and Mr. Ho inclined his head like a senator acknowledging the gallery.

"Mr. Ho," David said. "Diploma. Paper folded double. Did you know that?"

"I did know that," Mr. Ho said. "I taught the word for thirty-one years." He paused, and David braced for a lecture, but instead Mr. Ho only tapped the folder with one finger, gently, the way you'd touch a sleeping animal. "The Greeks folded a document so it sealed itself. Two halves agreeing to be one thing. I always thought that was the better half of the meaning." Then he got into his beige sedan and drove off before anyone could ask him anything else, which was, Alfred said, the most pedagogue move possible, like a magician who does one trick and leaves.

The lot was thinning. Tassels swung from rearview mirrors; somebody's little sister was eating a carnation; the school doors stood open and dark. Emerik sat down on the tailgate and looked at his truck like it was going to tell him something. In September he was moving to a town four hours north to work at his uncle's machine shop, no college, a decision he defended loudly at parties and defended to no one at all in private. "You'll come back at Thanksgiving," Alfred said, "and you'll be insufferable about having money."

"I'm insufferable now."

"You're insufferable now for free," David said. "Think of the upgrade."

Alfred was the one leaving farthest, a small college in Maine he'd chosen mostly, he admitted, because the brochure had a lake in it, and he had already packed his trunk so tightly that the lid bounced when he demonstrated it, slamming it twice for effect. He wanted them both to come to the diner in their gowns, one last plate of hash browns, one last booth by the window where they'd failed three quizzes' worth of studying. Emerik said no. Emerik said maybe. Emerik said somebody had to unload the truck by seven.

David closed his folder. He hadn't decided anything yet, not really; his own plan, such as it was, had seemed tenable in April, community college and living at home and transferring after two years, and now in the parking lot it felt smaller than it had in the kitchen with the acceptance letter on the table. He couldn't tell whether the plan had shrunk or whether he'd measured it wrong the first time, and he suspected he wouldn't know until he was two semesters into it, which was either a comforting thought or a terrible one.

He folded his diploma in half, carefully, along nothing, making the crease himself, and slid it into the folder, which now, he figured, held what it was supposed to hold.

"There," he said. "Fixed it."

"That's going to wreck the resale value," Emerik said, and Alfred laughed so hard the cap fell off, and David stood there holding the folder with both hands, like a tray, like something he'd finally been allowed to eat.

"So, hash browns," Alfred said, scooping the cap off the asphalt. "Both of you. I'm not asking again."

activity: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
knowledge_domain: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
fact: Freezer burn happens when air dries out the surface of frozen food; it makes food tough and tasteless but does not make it unsafe to eat.
story:
Oliver had learned the schedules first, before the knives or the pans, because Mr. Augustin said a kitchen that plans eats better than a kitchen that improvises. It was an odd thing to say, and Oliver had written it on the inside cover of his notebook, where he kept the grid he was building: seven dinners, one shopping list, two afternoons of cooking in batches. The restaurant kitchen where Mr. Augustin let him practice sat empty on Mondays, the ranges cold, the walk-in humming to itself, and Oliver had the long steel counter to himself until four o'clock.

He spread the week across the counter like a map. Chicken and rice on Monday, he had decided, because Monday needed something that forgave him if he was tired. Stew on Tuesday, made in a double batch on Sunday so that half could go into the freezer and become Friday's dinner without any work at all. He was proud of the arithmetic of it, the way eight hours of Sunday could be distributed across the week like money. His mother, working doubles at the hospital, had stopped cooking in November, and the two of them had been living on whatever was nearest. He wanted to change that, though he had not said so in exactly those words to anyone.

Mahmoud came in at three with a battered paper bag of spices from the shop near his house, which he set down next to Oliver's grid like an offering. "You're doing the whole week at once," he said, and there was admiration in it, but also a small frown, the kind he wore when he thought a plan had a hole in it. "My mum says cooking ahead is how food goes to waste. She says people forget what's in the freezer."

"My system has labels," Oliver said, and showed him the masking tape and the marker, the little rectangles of tape on empty containers already marked TUES and FRI, with dates underneath. Mahmoud ran a thumb over one of the labels and did not look convinced, but he unpacked the spices anyway, and together they browned the stew meat in the wide pan, Mahmoud voluble the whole time about his uncle who had run a kitchen in Alexandria and could make eight dishes from one chicken, a man Oliver privately thought of as a polymath of the pot.

They cooked until the light through the high windows went long and amber. The stew filled the kitchen with a smell of thyme and tomato, and Lili-Rose arrived near the end with her bike helmet still on, carrying a notebook of her own, because she had appointed herself the auditor of Oliver's plan. She read the grid, asked what he had budgeted for the shopping, and pointed out that he had priced the chicken from memory. "Memory is not a price," she said. They walked to the supermarket with a list, and Oliver wrote the real numbers down, and the total was eleven dollars more than he had guessed, which Lili-Rose noted without gloating.

The week began well. Monday's chicken was slightly overcooked but edible. Tuesday's stew, fresh, was better than edible, and his mother ate it standing at the counter and then sat down, which felt like an event. Wednesday Oliver was alone in the house, and he wrote a message to Mahmoud about it.

The message said: "She sat down at the table to eat. First time since November. Also, I think I messed up the freezer containers. The Friday one wasn't sealed right, I was rushing. The lid was sitting crooked and there's white dry stuff on the top of the stew now, grayish white, like frost but on the meat itself. Do we throw it out? That's like six dollars of food."

Mahmoud's reply came while Oliver was still holding his own phone in the cold breath of the open freezer. "My mum says that's freezer burn. Air dries out the surface. It makes food tough and tasteless but it doesn't make it unsafe to eat." Then a second message, shorter: "So you can eat it. Whether you'll want to is a different question."

Oliver stood there with the container in his hands, the frost-light patching the stew's surface like something weathered. Part of him, the part that made grids and printed labels, wanted to throw it out, to start clean, to treat the mistake as contamination. Another part, the part that had counted the eleven extra dollars, held on. He thought about how the plan was supposed to work, how it was supposed to make the week easier, and how a plan that wasted food whenever it hiccupped was not actually a plan, just a tidier kind of carelessness.

On Friday he thawed the stew and tasted it before seasoning it. The texture was tougher where the air had touched it, the flavor thinner, exactly as promised, and he stood at the stove adjusting, adding a splash of vinegar, a little more tomato paste, letting it go longer on low heat until it pulled itself back together into something worth sitting down for. It was not what Sunday had made. It was what Friday could rescue from Sunday, and he decided that counted.

Lili-Rose came by with her helmet hanging from her hand and ate a bowl of it at the table, since his mother had asked, through a note left by the kettle, that whoever ate on Friday eat at the table and not over the sink. She took a second helping without being asked, which was the only review Oliver needed. He wrote a new line on the inside cover of his notebook, under the first: press the lids down until they catch, all the way around. Then, after a moment, he added a second line, and put the pen down and carried his bowl to the sink while the last of the daylight went grey against the window over the stove.

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: Many news stories begin with a dateline naming the city where the story was reported, placed before the first sentence.
story:
Eric had told himself the language booth at the festival would be easy, the way he told himself most things would be easy, and by eleven in the morning he knew he had lied. Mr. Rosen stood behind a folding table stacked with foreign newspapers, clipboard in hand, signing off summaries for extra credit that Eric needed more than he would admit out loud. The rule was simple. Pick an article, read it, summarize it aloud in the new language, two minutes minimum, no English. Eric had chosen Portuguese because Saphira had said it wasn't that hard, and Saphira was rarely wrong, though she was blase about being right, which made it worse.

"Third time's yours," Linkin said, lounging against the tent pole with a churro he wasn't eating. Linkin had already gone with Spanish and cleared it in one try, and he kept finding reasons to stay near the table, which Eric pretended not to notice.

Eric spread the paper flat. The article was short, something about a bridge and a vote, and he worked through it word by word, finger under each line, sweating in a way he blamed on the October sun. Saphira drifted over, read over his shoulder for ten seconds, and said, "You're starting in the wrong place."

"I'm starting at the first word."

"That's what I mean."

He waved her off. He had his system, and his system had gotten him through four years of Spanish and one spectacularly mediocre semester of French. He read the first sentence twice, muttered a translation, and when he felt ready he turned to Mr. Rosen and began. "The article says that in Madrid the government voted..."

Mr. Rosen lowered his clipboard. "Madrid?"

"That's where the bridge is. I think."

Mr. Rosen tapped the paper once, above where Eric's finger had started, and Eric saw a line he had skipped entirely: two words before the first sentence, a city name, then a dash, then the sentence he'd been wrestling with. Not Madrid. Lisbon. He had read right past the part that told him where the story was from, because it sat before the part he'd decided counted as the beginning.

"That's the dateline," Saphira said. "Lots of news stories start with one. The city, then the story."

"You could have said that earlier."

"You could have listened earlier."

Mr. Rosen's voice stayed even, which was worse than if he'd been sharp. "Again from the top. You've got one more attempt before the lunch rush." He didn't say it was Eric's last attempt, but the line of students behind him said it for him.

Linkin leaned in while Eric regrouped, chewing now. "Want the number for the Lisbon bridge vote?"

"Shut up."

"I'm helping."

Eric ignored him, which took effort, and looked at the dateline again. It occurred to him, slowly, the way things occurred to him, that he had two habits pulling in opposite directions. There was the habit of charging straight at the first real sentence, treating everything before it as decoration, and there was the quieter habit Saphira had, of reading around a text before reading through it, letting the edges tell you what the middle would be about. He had always thought of her way as slowness, or showing off, or both. Standing there with the sun on the newsprint, he understood it as something else, though he couldn't have named it, and he was honest enough with himself, on a good day, to admit the understanding might not survive the walk home.

He also noticed something that sensitized him, as his mother would say, to how often he did this: skipped the front matter, opened the book at chapter one, answered the question without reading the prompt. A small peccadillo, maybe. Except the dateline was the story's passport, and he'd been summarizing a country the article never mentioned.

He started over. The dateline first, said out loud like a door opening. "Lisbon. The article is from Lisbon." Then the bridge, then the vote, then the part he still wasn't sure about, a phrase about money that could mean approved or proposed, and he said so, in clumsy Portuguese, in English, then Portuguese again, and Mr. Rosen wrote something down without telling him what.

"Close enough on the uncertain part," Mr. Rosen said finally, and initialed the clipboard. "Next."

Saphira was already gone toward the food stalls. Linkin held out the last of his churro.

"Half," Linkin said. "You earned half."

activity: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
knowledge_domain: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
fact: In the United States, a 100-year flood zone does not mean a flood every 100 years; it means the area has a 1 percent chance of flooding in any given year.
story:
The library's second-floor computer lab smelled of radiator dust and the burnt-coffee tang of the machine by the printing station, and Jackson had until six o'clock, when the lab closed, to learn enough geographic information system software to matter. Ms. Kerr had signed him in, shown him where the GIS license lived on the machine nearest the window, and told him that the tutorial videos had subtitles if the audio got away from him. Then she had gone back to the desk and left him to it, which he appreciated. He was sixteen and did not want to be taught so much as permitted.

The reason for the deadline was his mother. She had called at lunch, standing in the kitchen of a house on Delmar Street with the Realtor's voice going in the background, saying the seller had told her the neighborhood had never flooded and the listing said it was barely inside the hundred-year zone, so basically safe for a century. She wanted to put in an offer by tomorrow morning. Jackson had said "sure" and hung up and then sat very still at the cafeteria table, because something about the phrase had snagged in his mind, the way a word you have read a thousand times suddenly looks misspelled.

William was already at the lab when Jackson arrived, sprawled in the chair beside the window machine with his boots up on the spare stool, ostensibly working on the same assignment for Ms. Kerr's research seminar. Sunny came ten minutes later, carrying a notebook and a granola bar she immediately began eating in violation of at least two posted rules. The seminar project was theirs too: overlay the city's flood-risk layers on a housing layer and see what patterns fell out. It had been Sunny's idea to look at whether the impecunious parts of town sat in the wet ones, which she had phrased more delicately in the proposal, and which the data, so far, was confirming without delicacy at all.

Jackson followed the tutorial. He imported the parcel map, a pale grid of the whole city, then found the flood layer in the county's open data portal and dragged it on top. The special flood hazard area appeared as a hatched blue smear along the river, and where it crossed the parcels, the houses beneath it turned the color of a bruise. His hands were slow at first; he deleted the legend twice and had to undo it, and Sunny leaned over and said he was treating the software like it owed him money. But by the second hour he could query a parcel, and by the third he could type an address into the search bar without his pulse doing anything.

He typed Delmar Street. The map flew to the south side and settled, and there was his mother's maybe-house, a small polygon with a red outline, sitting inside the blue hatch like a beetle in netting. William rolled his chair over to look. "Barely inside," he said, reading the shape of it. "The corner of the lot kisses the zone."

Jackson opened a second browser tab, because the tutorial had not explained the name of the thing and the name was what bothered him. The Federal Emergency Management Agency page said it plainly, in the flat language of agencies: a hundred-year flood zone did not mean a flood every hundred years. It meant the area had a 1 percent chance of flooding in any given year. He read it twice. Then he said it out loud, quietly, to the screen. "A hundred-year flood zone means a one percent chance of flooding in any given year." Sunny stopped chewing. William's chair stopped rolling.

"So it could flood this year," Sunny said. "And next year. And the year after that."

"Or not for fifty years," Jackson said. "It's a coin the size of a year, and it's weighted ninety-nine to one, and they flip it every single year anyway." He was aware that he was doing something with the two ideas, the seller's safe-for-a-century version and the agency's version, holding them side by side and feeling which one had weight. The seller was not exactly lying, he decided. The seller was taking a piece of statistical language and letting it stand in the doorway of a house with its shoes on, burnishing a risk into a story people wanted to hear. Whether that was dishonesty or just the pragmatics of real estate, Jackson could not fully say, and he noticed that he could not fully say it and did not much like the noticing.

He called his mother from the lobby, under the poster about summer reading, with the automatic doors breathing open and shut behind him and cold air washing his ankles each time. He told her what the map showed, where the hatch fell on the lot, and then told her the thing itself: what the zone meant and did not mean. She was quiet for a moment. He could hear the Realtor somewhere behind her voice, bright and far away, saying something about charming original trim. His mother said she still wanted the house. She said she would ask about insurance in the morning, and maybe about a sump pump, and that she loved him, and that she'd bring home dinner.

Jackson stood in the doorway of the lobby a while after the call ended, watching the parking lot go amber under the streetlights, not sure whether he had helped or only complicated things. Then he went back upstairs, where Sunny had printed the overlaid map in tacky color and William was arguing with the print driver, and he sat down and started labeling the parcels in the blue hatch, one address at a time, because the assignment was still due, and the lab closed at six.

activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
knowledge_domain: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
fact: The AP 2-D Art and Design portfolio's Sustained Investigation section asks for 15 digital images and counts for 60 percent of the score.
story:
Gabrielle had taped her ten thumbnails to the studio window in a grid, three across and four down with two gaps, and she was standing back with her coffee going cold when Thea came in shaking rain off her jacket. "Is that the portfolio," Thea said, not quite a question, and Gabrielle said it was, ten pieces on doors, all the doors she'd photographed since September: the metal one at the pool, her grandmother's screen door with the torn patch shaped like a hand, the janitor's closet at school that someone had covered in stickers. Ten felt complete. Ten felt like a number a person could hold.

Thea dropped her bag on the paint-splattered table and pulled out her phone. "You're doing this for AP, right? The 2-D one." Gabrielle said she was, that Mr. Korhonen had told her class in the fall that the college credit was worth the spring of work, and that she'd been planning ever since. Thea scrolled, frowning, then turned the screen around. "It says fifteen."

Gabrielle took the phone. The page was dense with language about inquiry and practice, but the numbers stood out plainly: the Sustained Investigation section asked for fifteen digital images, and that section counted for sixty percent of the score. She read it twice, then a third time, because the numbers refused to rearrange themselves into something kinder. Fifteen. Sixty percent. She had built her whole spring around ten, had told her mother ten, had turned down the spring musical for ten.

"That can't be right," she said, but it was right there with a logo at the top, and Thea, who had already survived one AP exam and wore that knowledge like a badge, just raised her eyebrows. "Fifteen images," Thea said. "Sustained Investigation. It's the big part."

Ethen was in the back room stretching canvas, and when Gabrielle carried the phone to him he wiped his hands on his jeans and studied it with the truculent expression he wore whenever an authority of any kind, a teacher, a referee, a magistrate on a courtroom show, told him what to do. "So they want more than you've got," he said. "So you make more." He said it as though the solution were obvious and slightly offensive, which was how Ethen said most things.

But it wasn't obvious, and that was the problem she carried around for the next week. Ten doors was an idea, a closed argument; fifteen doors risked becoming wallpaper, repetition for repetition's sake. She had chosen doors because they were thresholds, because a door is both a barrier and an invitation depending on which side you're standing on, and she had made each piece hinge, literally in two cases, on that double meaning. Adding five more felt like it could dilute the whole, like a sentence extended past its period. She said as much to Mr. Korhonen on Thursday, when he came through the studio with his mug and his habit of stopping at her window.

"Show me the grid," he said, and she did, and he looked for a long time at the two empty spaces at the bottom. Then he asked her which piece had taken the most drafts, and she pointed to the fourth one, the screen door, which had gone through six versions before she'd stopped trying to paint the tear and instead cut the paper so the viewer could lift it. He nodded and moved on to Ethen's canvas without offering anything further, which was his way, and she spent the walk home annoyed at him and then, somewhere around the bridge, less annoyed.

Because the question he'd actually asked was about process, and the AP page had said images, not artworks. Fifteen digital images. Sitting at her desk with her sketchbook open, she looked back through the six versions of the screen door, the photographs of the maquette, the failed first attempt she'd photographed before gessoing over it, and understood, slowly, the way you understand a word you've been mispronouncing, that the investigation could include the investigating. The five additional images didn't have to be five new doors. They could be the record of her thinking, which was, she admitted, the part of the work she actually loved and had been hiding.

This didn't settle everything. She still had to write the artist's statement, and her first draft that night was two sentences that sounded like a magistrate delivering a verdict, cold and official, and she deleted it. She still didn't know whether the strongest pieces were the ones where the idea showed or the ones where it hid. And somewhere under all of it was the smaller, quieter loss: she had liked the tidiness of ten, and tidiness was gone now, replaced by something messier that invigorated her and exhausted her in almost equal measure.

On Saturday she came in early, before Thea or Ethen, and moved the two chairs away from the window so the morning light fell straight on her grid. She unrolled a fresh sheet of paper across the table, weighted the corners with paint tubes, and began laying out the six versions of the screen door in a row, oldest to newest, photographing each one as she went. Behind her, the studio radiator ticked. In front of her, the torn patch shaped like a hand lifted slightly in the draft from the door she'd propped open.

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: In translation, the ribosome moves along the messenger RNA and joins amino acids together with peptide bonds to build a protein chain.
story:
Chloe had taped the diagram to her bedroom wall three days before the exam, and by now she had almost habituated to it, the way one habituates to a poster of a band one no longer listens to. It showed a fat squiggle marked DNA, an arrow labeled transcription, a thinner strand labeled mRNA, a second arrow labeled translation, and at the bottom a chain of little circles called amino acids. Somewhere in the middle of all that, according to her textbook, a structure called a ribosome did the actual work, and that was where her understanding dissolved into fog. She had a scholarship interview in two weeks, in which a biochemistry professor would ask her to explain the central dogma from memory, and her mother had already told two neighbors about it, which meant backing out was no longer a private option.

At seven on Thursday evening, Reet arrived at the front door carrying a bag of clementines and her own crumpled copy of the same diagram. "Mr. Ramos says if I fail this unit I fail the course," she announced, toeing off her shoes in the hallway. "So I figured you'd tutor me and also we could eat these." She was not a close friend, exactly; she was mercurial, generous one week and distant the next, and Chloe had spent most of the school year keeping her at a careful middle distance. But Reet's mother worked nights, and their kitchen table was empty, and Chloe's kitchen table had two chairs nobody was using.

They spread out on the living room carpet because the table was covered with Chloe's mother's paperwork, a stack of documents relating to some dispute with the landlord that had lately involved the word subpoena, which their mother kept saying with grim satisfaction, as though it were a weapon she had finally learned to hold. Chloe pushed the papers into a neater pile and laid out the diagram between them.

"Okay," Chloe said. "Transcription first. The DNA is the master copy, and the cell can't use it directly, so it makes a photocopy. The photocopy is mRNA. That's transcription." Reet peeled a clementine in one long spiral, which Chloe privately envied, and nodded with the expression of someone who had heard this four times already from four different people.

"Then translation," Chloe said, and stopped. The fog rolled in on schedule. "The mRNA gets read, and a protein gets made, and I always lose the middle part."

"The middle part is the part he'll ask about," Reet said, not unkindly. She pulled a shoelace from her bag, actual shoelace, and a sandwich bag of beads she must have taken from her little brother's craft box. "I've been trying it like this. Tell me if I'm wrong."

She laid the shoelace along the mRNA on the diagram and began threading beads onto it, one at a time, sliding each one down the string while glancing at a strip of paper beside her on which she'd written a sequence of letters. "The shoelace is the message," she said. "The beads are the amino acids. My fingers are, um." She frowned at her own hands.

"Wait," Chloe said. She was looking at the diagram's blobby gray ribosome, then at Reet's fingers pinching the string, then at the growing line of beads. "Your fingers. The ribosome is your fingers. It's the thing that moves along the mRNA and joins the amino acids together while it reads." Reet threaded another bead, and Chloe watched the chain lengthen. "And the connections between the beads. Those are real things, they have a name. Peptide bonds." She said it and then checked the textbook, because she didn't trust herself yet, and there it was in figure 14.3, the same word. "The ribosome moves along the messenger RNA and joins the amino acids together with peptide bonds, and the whole string of them is the protein."

Reet held up the beaded shoelace, which was now a floppy multicolored worm. "So this is a protein."

"That's a protein."

"And the order of the beads matters because of the letters on the paper."

"Because of the mRNA, yes." Chloe took the shoelace from her and ran it through her fingers, beads clicking. For the first time the diagram on the wall looked less like a foreign map and more like a set of instructions, something a person could actually do with her hands. She tried saying the whole thing again from DNA onward, without the book, and got through it, and Reet clapped twice, the way she did at swim meets.

From the kitchen doorway, Reet watched Chloe say it a second time, slower, correcting herself once on the order of the bonds. There was something in the way Chloe insisted on getting it exactly right, the way she kept going even after being applauded, that made Reet feel both embarrassed and steadied, like she'd been let into a room where people simply did the work. She thought about telling her that Mr. Ramos had actually said Chloe was the one at risk of failing, that the tutoring had been his idea and Chloe's mother had arranged it over the phone on Sunday, but the clementines were sweet and the beads were still scattered across the carpet, and she had habituated, over many years, to letting certain truths wait.

"Again," Reet said, scooping the beads back into the bag. "From the top. And this time I get to be the ribosome."

Chloe laughed, picked up the shoelace, and read out the first three letters.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Pencil 'lead' has never been made of the metal lead; the name comes from the 16th century, when graphite was mistaken for a kind of lead ore.
story:
The last weekend before the sale, Cameron spread his materials across his grandfather's workbench in the garage: a pad of heavy paper, a tin of pencils graded from 9H to 8B, a kneaded eraser going gray from use. He was drawing the house. Not a photograph of it, which his mother could take on her phone, but a drawing, because a drawing took hours and hours meant sitting with the porch rail, the leaning fence post, the screen door that had to be lifted slightly to close. The realtor's sign went up on Monday. He had two days.

He had brought Julie because she was the best draftsman in their class and because she said things other people didn't think to say. She stood in the driveway squinting at the roofline, arms crossed, and the first thing she told him was that he was drawing it wrong. Too even, she said. Every shingle the same size, every shadow polite. "You're trying to make it deserve being remembered," she said. "That's not the same as looking at it."

Cameron argued, quietly, because his grandmother was napping inside and the garage door was open. He said accuracy was a kind of love, that if he got the proportions of the porch steps right, if the perspective of the fence converged the way it actually converged, then the drawing would hold something true. Julie said truth wasn't the same as measurement. She pulled his pad toward her and blocked in the fence with six loose strokes that looked more like the fence than his twenty careful ones. He took the pad back. They were still friends, but the workbench between them had become a border.

His little cousin found him there after lunch, an eight-year-old who had been told to stay out of everyone's way and had interpreted this generously. She planted herself on the stool by the vise and watched him sharpen a pencil with a knife, which she declared the coolest thing she had ever seen. Then, while Cameron was measuring the windows, she put the sharpened end in her mouth and bit it, experimentally, the way a person tests a pen cap.

"Spit it out," Cameron said, more sharply than he meant to, and she did, and then her eyes filled. She said the kids at school said you could die from lead poisoning, that a boy in her class had to go to the hospital, that pencils had lead in them, everybody knew that, it was called lead. She was working herself toward real crying, the kind that coagulates the whole face into red.

Cameron knelt down, which felt ridiculous and which he did anyway. "It's not that kind of lead," he said. "It's never been the metal. Pencil lead has always been graphite." She said graphite like a foreign word, and he said it again, slower. "The name comes from the sixteenth century. People found graphite and thought it was a kind of lead ore. They were wrong, but the name stayed." She asked if he was sure, and he said he was sure, and he was; he'd looked it up once in ninth grade after an art teacher had said it offhandedly and he hadn't believed her. She wiped her nose on her sleeve and asked if she could have the sharpened pencil, since it wasn't poison, and he gave it to her.

Julie had watched all this from the stool by the vise, and afterward she said, "You're like that with the drawing too, you know. Someone tells you a thing and you have to go verify it before you'll act." Cameron expected her to be mocking him, but she wasn't. She turned his pad around again and pointed at the porch. "That's not a weakness. I'm the opposite. I just decide and go. You could call me an ideologue of looseness. Which is embarrassing, actually, when the fence looks like that." Her fence did look like that, blurry and alive, and his did not.

They worked through the afternoon and Cameron tried something he would not have tried alone. He kept his measured scaffolding, the converging lines, the proportions he'd checked twice, and inside it he let himself be less polite. He drew the porch rail where it sagged instead of where it should have been. He left the shadow under the eaves dark and unresolved. It went against his instinct the whole time, like writing with his left hand, and somewhere in the last hour the two ways of working stopped fighting each other. He couldn't have said which parts were Julie's method and which were his. He wasn't sure the distinction even held up anymore, though he suspected it did, somewhere, and that he just couldn't find the seam.

His grandmother came out near sunset with glasses of lemonade and stood behind them for a long moment without speaking. She was not normally an effusive woman; she said thank you once and meant it for a decade. When she did speak, it was to the drawing and not to him, which he understood to be the highest compliment available to her. "The screen door," she said. "You even got the lifting." She set the lemonade down on the workbench, directly on a pencil he had left there, and walked back inside with her hand on the doorframe for a moment longer than she needed.

Julie left first, taking the pencils she'd borrowed and telling him the drawing was better than both of them, which was either generous or accurate. Cameron stayed to clean the workbench, sorting the pencils by grade, blowing graphite dust off his grandfather's old square. He didn't know if the drawing was a real record or a real picture or whether those were even different things, and he rolled the pad closed without deciding. He carried it through the screen door, lifting it slightly as he went, the way it had always needed to be lifted.

activity: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
knowledge_domain: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
fact: In the far North Atlantic, the water cools and becomes dense enough to sink, then flows south deep underwater as part of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation.
story:
Victor had agreed to the presentation before he understood what he had agreed to. Mr. Thompson wanted ten minutes on ocean currents, delivered without slides, "as if you were telling a friend something interesting," which sounded kind until Victor realized it meant he actually had to understand the material. He had a week. His parents had already planned the weekend at his grandfather's house on the coast, so the maps came with him: folded charts of the North Atlantic, printed in blues and reds, spread across the kitchen table while his grandfather puttered around making coffee and pretending not to look.

"Red means warm," Victor said to himself, tracing the band that swept up the American coast and then bent east across the ocean. That much he knew. The Gulf Stream carried warm water north, and somehow this was why London, sitting at the same latitude as Newfoundland, had rain instead of ice. But the arrow just kept going north, and if warm water kept traveling into a cold sea, what stopped it? The charts showed nothing. They ended, like the explanation he had prepared, in the middle of the Greenland Sea.

He remembered the science museum in the city, the trip from two years ago with Libby and Myriam. There had been a screen on the wall, an animation of the Atlantic in cross-section, and he had stood in front of it mostly because Libby was standing in front of it. A red current rose through the middle of the ocean like smoke. Then, in the far north, the red had faded, and the water turned blue and dropped, sliding down and flowing back south along the floor of the ocean, a slow river under the surface. He had watched it loop twice and thought it was beautiful without thinking about it at all.

"Grandpa," he said, "when you fished up north, was the water different down deep?"

His grandfather set down his cup. "Different how?"

"Colder. Heavier, maybe."

His grandfather considered this the way he considered most things, slowly, with his eyes on the window and the gray water beyond it. "The trawlers talk about layers," he said. "Top water and deep water don't mix like you'd expect. That's all I know. Don't prevaricate to an old man, now. Say what you're asking."

Victor laughed and spread the charts flat. "I'm asking why the warm water doesn't just pile up in the north." He pressed his finger on the Greenland Sea. "It goes here, it cools off, it gets dense enough to sink. Then it flows back south. Deep. Underwater, all the way back." Saying it aloud, he felt the animation and the chart click together, two pictures of one thing. "Libby would call it the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation," he added. "She memorized the name in the car on the way to the museum. She likes knowing what things are called."

His grandfather grunted and pulled a chair over, which surprised Victor, who had expected an interminable afternoon of polite nodding. The old man studied the chart for a long time. "So the ocean turns over," he said. "Like a pot."

"Sort of," Victor said, and then, honestly, "I don't know how the whole thing works. I know the water sinks here and flows south, and I know the name for the circulation. Why it starts, what keeps it going, whether it's slowing down, people argue about all of that. I can't explain what I don't understand."

"You could have just made something up," his grandfather said. "Plenty do."

"I'd rather say I don't know. Mr. Thompson says a good explanation includes its own edges."

The weekend passed with the charts on the table, Victor rehearsing in the mornings while his grandfather washed dishes and offered corrections that had nothing to do with oceanography and everything to do with standing still and not rushing. On Sunday night, back home, Victor got a message from Myriam: Mr. Thompson was out sick Monday, the presentations postponed until further notice, possibly cancelled. Victor stared at it, feeling the week of work go loose and strange in his hands, and was still holding the phone when a second message arrived from his grandfather, typed slowly in full sentences with his index fingers.

The fishing club meets Thursday, the message said. Six old men who argue about the sea every week and get it wrong. Come and tell them about the water that sinks. Bring the charts.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: In 1977 Tuckman and Mary Ann Jensen added a fifth stage, adjourning, for when a group's work ends and members separate.
story:
The gym smelled like rubber and cold pizza, and somebody had taped a banner over the entrance that said SEASON ENDS, PEOPLE DON'T, which Ms. Chaudhry had clearly made on her own printer. I sat on the bleachers with my shoes still laced, because taking them off felt like agreeing that it was over. We had lost the semifinal by four points two nights ago, and Kellyann had not spoken much since, and Libby had brought a cake shaped like a basketball that was collapsing in the middle in the heat.

"You have to try the cake," Libby said, pressing a plate toward me. "It's the last cake. That's the whole thing about it."

I took the plate. The seniors were gathered at the far basket, Kellyann and two others, shooting free throws with a laziness that didn't portend anything except more free throws. There was no game left for them to save their legs for. Kellyann's form had gone loose and pretty, the follow-through held a second longer than it needed to be, like she was admiring the shape of it.

Ms. Chaudhry clapped twice from midcourt. "Circle up. Bring the cake, bring whatever."

We sat on the floor in a ring at the three-point line. She had a plastic bag of paper awards, best defender, most improved, and she handed them out with commentary that was mostly insults wrapped in affection. When she got to Kellyann, she paused.

"Four years," Ms. Chaudhry said. "I've never had a point guard who argued with me more, and I've never had one I trusted more."

Kellyann looked at the floor and picked at a seam in the wood. I kept thinking about something I'd read in the psychology book my brother left in the bathroom, the one he used for his college course. Teams were groups, obviously, but groups apparently had stages, and I had looked it up on my phone on the bus home from the semifinal because I wanted to know if what I was feeling had a name.

"Ms. Chaudhry," I said. "Did you know groups have stages? Forming, storming, norming, performing."

"I've heard of it," she said. "Tuckman."

"In 1977 Tuckman and Mary Ann Jensen added a fifth stage," I said. "Adjourning. For when a group's work ends and members separate."

Nobody said anything for a second. Libby mouthed adjourning at me like she was tasting it.

"So that's what this is," Kellyann said. "Adjourning. This party. This is a whole stage of development."

"You're adjourning," Libby told her. "We're just losing you."

"Same thing," Kellyann said, but she was smiling a little, and she reached over and straightened the ribbon on my plate even though it didn't need straightening.

Natalie watched her do it. She thought about how she had spent the season wanting two things that pulled against each other: she had wanted the seniors to take the team seriously, to run the plays right, to treat Tuesday practices like they mattered, and she had also wanted to be like them, unbothered, above it. Watching Kellyann now, loose-armed at the free throw line, laughing at a bad pass instead of glaring at it, she understood that Kellyann had been doing the second thing all along, and that it had never been carelessness. It had been the freedom of knowing the clock.

"You could coach," Natalie said to her. "Little kids. They'd pay you."

"Remuneration for yelling at people," Kellyann said. "My dream job."

"I'm serious. You're good at the explaining part."

Kellyann bounced the ball once, caught it, and looked at the far wall where the championship banners hung, none of them theirs. "Maybe," she said. "Ask me in August."

The lights were on a timer, and halfway through the second cake one bank of them cut out with a clunk, leaving the near half of the court bright and the far half dim, the banners going gray and diaphanous in the distance, hard to read from where they sat. Nobody moved to find the switch. The party had drifted to that point where everyone is waiting for someone else to stand up first.

Natalie thought that forming, storming, norming, performing made sense to her; she could match each one to a month of the season. Adjourning was harder. She didn't feel like she was separating from anything yet, because in September there would be a team, and a gym, and probably a cake. What she couldn't figure was whether the group coming back would be the same group, or whether the group, this specific one with Libby's collapsing cake and Kellyann's long follow-through, had already ended on the buzzer two nights ago and this was just the paperwork. She decided she could hold both of those ideas at once without picking, which was either wisdom or laziness, and she didn't have a way to tell which.

Kellyann stood, brushed crumbs off her shorts, and picked up the ball.

"One game," she said. "Seniors versus everybody. First to eleven."

"You'll lose," Libby said.

"Then you'll have beaten a legend."

They ran to half court, and the lights on the far side came back on all at once, bright enough that the whole floor showed, every scuff and every name scrawled in the key by some team from years before theirs.

activity: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
knowledge_domain: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
fact: At a Seder, a piece of the middle matzah called the afikoman is set aside, often hidden for children to find, and eaten as the last food of the meal.
story:
William arrived at his aunt's house with a grocery bag of matzah, a photocopy of the Haggadah, and the knot in his stomach he'd been carrying since he volunteered. His grandmother had led the Seder for thirty years, and this spring she could not; her hands shook too badly to hold the book. When he'd offered, over the phone, she'd said only, "Good," which either allayed his fear or simply refused to feed it.

His friends had wanted to come. Adeline, who was curious about everything she'd never seen, and Cullen, who was mostly curious about brisket. His aunt had said of course, the more the better, and now the table was set for eleven, the candles waiting, and William standing at the head with a sheet of notes he had rewritten three times.
