He got through the beginning better than expected. He asked the Four Questions in Hebrew his grandmother corrected gently, one syllable at a time, and he explained the salt water and the bitter herb. When his youngest cousin demanded the story of the ten plagues again, he acted out the frogs with more enthusiasm than dignity, and even his uncle, who could turn bellicose about politics by the second glass of wine, laughed and let the subject drop.

The meal itself was easy. His aunt carried out the soup, the brisket, the flourless chocolate cake Adeline had brought, and for an hour William was just a nephew and a host, refilling glasses, coaxing his grandmother to eat. It was during the clearing that he looked down at his notes and felt the floor tilt. The afikoman, the broken half of the middle matzah he was supposed to have set aside and hidden for the children to find, was still sitting in the matzah box. He had read the line in his preparation, that the meal could not end until it was found and eaten as the last food of the night, and then he had skipped it entirely.

He stepped into the pantry and called Cullen, who answered with his mouth full. "The afikoman," William whispered. "It's a piece of the middle matzah. You break it, hide it, the kids hunt for it, and it has to be the last thing eaten. I never hid it." There was a pause, then Cullen said, "So hide it now, genius," which was not elegant but was, William had to admit, correct. The problem was the children were already at the table, and the house had no rooms they couldn't see into.

He stalled with songs. He led three rounds of "Dayenu" at increasing speed, and while the table roared the third chorus he slipped into the kitchen, broke the middle matzah, and cast around for a hiding place. The oven was warm and wrong. The fridge was visible from the hallway. In the end he wedged it inside the roasting pan drawer beneath the oven, wiped his hands, and returned to announce, with the gravity of a man declaring a theocracy's founding, that the great hunt had begun.

The children tore through the house. His cousin's daughter checked behind the couch cushions with the thoroughness of a customs officer. Adeline pretended to search the bookshelf while obviously angling to see where William's eyes went, which was unhelpful, since William was staring at the ceiling to avoid staring at the oven. When the youngest finally found it, shrieking, in the drawer, William offered the traditional reward, and his uncle suggested five dollars, and William, who had not thought that far, had to admit the treasury consisted of whatever was in his coat.

"Then give her the coat," his grandmother said.

"She can have it," William said, and meant it, and his cousin's daughter wore his jacket through the dessert course like a robe of state. The afikoman was broken into small pieces and passed around, everyone chewing slowly, because it was the last food of the night and after it, nothing more. Even Cullen ate his piece without a single joke about cardboard.

It was later, washing dishes, that Adeline leaned against the counter beside him. "You know," she said, drying the good platter, "your grandmother came in from the kitchen right before the singing started. She was gone a while." William went still, dish dripping. He thought of the pantry phone call, the two minutes he'd spent in the kitchen, the years his grandmother had hidden that same piece in that same house. "You think she hid one first," he said, "and I hid a second one." Adeline opened the oven drawer, and there, behind where his piece had been, sat a second wrapped half of matzah, waiting all evening for a search that never came.

activity: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
knowledge_domain: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
fact: A coda is an optional closing section after the recapitulation that reinforces the home key and brings the movement to an end.
story:
The garage smelled of motor oil and old paper, because Mr. Pelletier had never fully moved his piano out of the part of the garage where the car used to go. The car now lived in the driveway, which the neighbors had opinions about, and Laurie's mother had opinions about the neighbors, and everyone agreed on nothing except that the piano should stay. Laurie came on Thursdays after school. Her mother called the ten dollars an honorarium, and Mr. Pelletier accepted it with the gravity of a man being paid in a currency he did not quite believe in.

"Exposition, development, recapitulation," he said, laying out the score of the Mozart on the piano rack. "That is the map. Your job is to draw the borders."

Laurie had brought sticky notes, three colors, because Elsie had told her that color coding was the difference between passing and humiliation, and had used the word "stigmatize" to describe what would happen to anyone who showed up to the exam with unannotated music. Elsie used that word a lot. Laurie had stopped arguing with it the way you stop arguing with weather.

She placed the first note herself. The opening theme arrived so plainly, so assertively in its own key, that the exposition marked itself; it was the part of Mozart that got used in commercials, which was a thing she decided not to say out loud. The second theme came in the new key, higher and more chatty, like the exposition had brought a friend. Mr. Pelletier said nothing, which she had learned was his version of approval, or possibly of sleep.

The development was harder, and she liked it harder. The themes went somewhere else entirely, pulled apart and reassembled, the opening idea turned upside down over a grinding bass, and for a moment the music seemed to have forgotten where it lived. She put the yellow note at measure 73 and Mr. Pelletier raised one finger, which meant she was close but wrong. She moved it to 75. The finger came down.

Then the opening theme returned, exactly itself, in the home key, and she pressed the last sticky note onto the page with real satisfaction. Recapitulation. Three sections, three notes, the map complete, four minutes of a five-minute movement accounted for. She sat back on the bench and waited to be told she was finished.

The music kept going.

She counted the measures with her pencil tip like a cashier counting bills that refused to add up. Sixteen bars past her last note, the piano was still playing, hammering the home key chord over and over, loud and final and obviously not development, not exposition, not anything her three colors knew about. The afternoon light came through the garage door cracks and lay alluvial across the concrete, dusty and spread thin, and she looked at it instead of at the score because the score was betraying her.

"That part," she said finally. "What's that part called?"

"What do you think it's doing?"

"Ending. Emphatically. It's like the movement is still talking after the sentence is over."

Mr. Pelletier made a small sound that in a lesser man would have been a chuckle. "A coda," he said. "Optional. Not every movement has one. It comes after the recapitulation and drives the home key home until the thing is finished for good."

"Optional," Laurie repeated. She looked at her three colors, at the sixteen unmarked measures, at the whole system she had trusted to be complete. She had liked the form best when it was a form, when it held. But she could see it the other way too, the way the coda made the ending a decision instead of a formality, and she could not decide which version of Mozart she believed in, so she took out her pencil instead of a fourth sticky note and wrote the word directly on the score.

Emma was in the driveway when Laurie came out, sitting on the hood of the exiled car with her own theory homework. "Did he explain sonata form?" Emma called. "I still don't get the development."

"It's where the music forgets its address," Laurie said. "I'll explain on the way. Bring your pencil."

Emma slid off the hood and held the car door for her like a chauffeur, and they walked toward the corner arguing about whether forgetting your address counted as a plot.

activity: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
knowledge_domain: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
fact: K. Anders Ericsson and colleagues' 1993 study of violinists described 'deliberate practice': effortful work on specific weaknesses with immediate feedback, not just logging hours.
story:
The cones were still in the mesh bag when Leo arrived, and the U12s were already scrimmaging, which was exactly the problem. Nine days till the regional friendly, and every Tuesday and Thursday since August they had done the same thing: two nets, one ball, forty minutes of chasing. They loved it. Their passing stayed terrible.

"You're late," Karis said, sitting on the folded chair with the attendance clipboard. She had arranged to be his assistant because, she claimed, watching him fail would be entertaining. "Also your fly is up, which today counts as good news."

"Mr. Ba's fence was down and the sheep got onto the road. I had to walk them back." He dropped the bag and watched a boy named Tommo hoof the ball thirty yards to no one. "Did anyone complete a pass in the first ten minutes?"

"Define complete."

"Someone intended it and someone received it."

Karis made a mark on her clipboard that was clearly a zero.

Leo had volunteered for this because his ankle had ended his own season in June and Coach had said, if you can't play, learn the other side of it. He had assumed the other side of it was picking teams and yelling encouragement. Instead it was this: nine ten-year-olds whose touches bounced off them like the ball was hot, and a match in nine days that his father, unhelpfully, had already told the neighbours about.

He called them in. "New plan. No scrimmage today." The groan came as one body, so loud that Mr. Ba, hauling fence wire at the far hedge, straightened up to see what was dying. Leo pushed through it. "Three groups. Karis takes shooting. I take passing."

"What's passing practice," Tommo said, not as a question, "going to be running in lines?"

It was going to be running in lines, more or less, and it went badly, and afterward Leo sat on the bus with his chemistry flashcards, unable to allay the suspicion that he had made everything worse. Enthalpy: the heat content of a system at constant pressure. He knew it for Monday's test and could not, at the moment, see why anyone cared. He thumbed past it and opened his phone instead and typed, almost as a joke, why does my team not get better.

He had expected forums. What he found was an article about violinists. In 1993, a researcher named K. Anders Ericsson and his colleagues had studied violinists and described something they called deliberate practice: effortful work on a specific weakness, with immediate feedback, as opposed to just logging hours. Leo read it twice. The violinists who were best had not simply played more; they had isolated what they did badly and drilled that, with someone telling them, right away, what had gone wrong. He thought of forty minutes of scrimmage, of nobody ever being told anything, and felt the shape of his mistake. It was not a comfortable feeling. It was also, he had to admit, a little exciting, though he couldn't yet say whether the excitement was trustworthy or just the relief of having a word for failure.

By the time Calista slid into the seat beside him at the next practice, he had a clipboard of his own, gridded and coded. She had heard about the cone lines from her brother, who played midfield, and had come to see for herself.

"So what happened Tuesday," she said, "was running."

"Tuesday was wrong." He showed her the grid. "Watch this." He set up a square of cones, six meters a side, three boys inside, one pressing. The rule was two touches, maximum; every pass had to be to a foot, not to a postcode; and Karis stood at the edge calling out each error as it happened, receive it, that was your body open, too heavy. When Tommo lunged at a ball and poked it out, Karis restarted the count before Tommo had finished turning. Tommo's face flushed. He asked for the ball again immediately, which he had never once done in scrimmage.

Calista watched a while, arms crossed against the wind. "He hates it," she said.

"He hates scrimmage more. He just doesn't know it, because in scrimmage nobody notices when you fail." Leo blew the whistle, tightened the square. "Here he fails forty times in ten minutes and knows every one."

They ran it until the light went yellow at the hedge line. Mr. Ba had finished his fence and stood leaning on the gate, saying nothing, which Leo had learned was the neighbour's highest form of approval. On Saturday they would scrimmage, once, at the end, as reward and as test, and Leo still did not know if nine days of squares could repair four months of chaos. The article had said nothing about ten-year-olds, or about coaches with sprained ankles and chemistry tests on Monday.

Thursday, Calista arrived early and found him taping cones. "My brother says the passing is actually better," she said. "He said it like it annoyed him."

Leo straightened. "Nobody's told me anything."

"Nobody will. They're ten." She picked up a stack of pinnies. "Square drills again?"

"Square drills, but smaller. Two touches to one." He shouldered the bag and started for the far touchline, where the boys were already fighting over a ball.

activity: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
knowledge_domain: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
fact: A simple random sample of about 1,000 people gives a margin of error of roughly plus or minus 3 percentage points for the whole sample's results.
story:
Jayden set his laptop beside his plate and ate one-handed while the pasta went cold. The school board race had been his story for six weeks, and tomorrow was press night, and the number on his screen would not sit still. Sixty-two percent of likely voters, the poll said, favored the incumbent. Thirty-eight percent favored the challenger, Gwenyth's cousin.

His father came in with mail under his arm and read the screen upside down from the sink. "Sixty-two. That's over. Write it and sleep."

"It's a thousand people," Jayden said. "I don't know what a thousand people tells you about a whole district."

"It tells you sixty-two percent, apparently." His father opened a bill, tore the envelope badly, and got choleric about it, swearing at the paper as if it had insulted him on purpose. Jayden waited him out. He had been inured to that particular sound since childhood, the sharp exhale, the second, harder tear.

He scrolled to the methodology page the polling class had printed for him. He read it twice, chewing nothing. A simple random sample of about 1,000 people, the page said, gives a margin of error of roughly plus or minus 3 percentage points for the whole sample's results. He copied the sentence into his notes, then sat looking at it while his father ran water over a pan that did not need washing.

Charly called while Jayden was carrying his plate to the sink. "Did you see it? Are we going with 'Incumbent Cruising'?"

"Where'd you get 'cruising.'"

"I made it up. It's good. It's a verb and it's an adjective."

Jayden balanced the phone against the soap dispenser and put the plate down. "Listen. A thousand people. Margin of error, plus or minus three points. So sixty-two could be fifty-nine, could be sixty-five. That part's fine, the race isn't close anyway. But the poll also has the incumbent at fifty-one among voters under thirty. Fifty-one to forty-nine." He heard Charly's chair creak on the other end. "Fifty-one is inside the three. The young-voter number could be a tie. Could be behind. I can't headline it."

"So cut the young-voter part."

"If I cut it, the story says the district loves the incumbent, full stop. That's not what the poll says. The poll says the district loves the incumbent, and the young-voter split is a coin we can't see."

Charly was quiet long enough that Jayden checked whether the call had dropped. Then Charly said, "Ms. Mercer's going to ask why the number's in the story if we can't say what it means."

"Then we say what it means. Fifty-one, plus or minus three. The reader can hold both."

"That's not a headline, Jayden. That's existentialism."

"It's not existentialism. It's arithmetic." But he laughed, and Charly laughed, and the fight went out of it the way it did between them, sideways.

He carried the phone back to the table and sat down across from where his father had been. The methodology page was still open. He tested the sentence against the other numbers: the overall result, sixty-two, sat well outside the three-point margin, and a twenty-four-point lead did not need hedging. That he could print in forty-point type with a clean conscience. The rest he would run lower, in the body, with the caveat attached and the sample size stated, and readers could decide for themselves whether fifty-one meant momentum or noise.

His father came back for coffee and stood reading over his shoulder again, which he only did when he wanted to be asked. "So it's over," his father said.

"The big number, yes. The under-thirty number, nobody knows."

"Then why print what nobody knows."

"Because not knowing is the finding," Jayden said, and typed it before he could talk himself out of it: Incumbent Holds Wide Lead; Young Voters Split Within Poll's Margin of Error. He read it once, out loud, quietly, to the empty chair and the cooling coffee.

"Still not a verb," Charly said from the phone.

activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
knowledge_domain: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
fact: In the United States the Federal Reserve's main policy rate is the federal funds rate, the rate banks charge each other for overnight loans of reserves.
story:
The laptop showed Riley his own face in the corner of the call, chin propped on his fist, and in the main window Elyse held up a flashcard that read, in her handwriting, WHY DOES THE FED HURT EVERYONE ON PURPOSE. Riley had forty hours until his econ presentation, and so far his best explanation was "money gets expensive, I guess," which had not satisfied anyone, least of all him.

"Say it like you're talking to your mom," Leonie said from her tile. "Your mom is smart but she thinks the Fed is a building."

The problem was that Riley had been treating it like a building. Two days earlier he had stood in line at the bank to deposit his paycheck from the garden center, and a television bolted to the ceiling had announced that the Fed was raising rates again. He had asked the teller, mostly to be social, which rate the Fed actually set. "The federal funds rate," she had said. "It's the rate banks charge each other for overnight loans of reserves." She said it the way someone recites a fact learned in training and never needed since, and Riley had nodded as though he'd known that, which was a habit his mother called his most reliable skill.

At home he kept circling back to that sentence. He'd assumed the Fed set some rate that regular people paid, mortgages or credit cards, a lever wired straight to his own declining balance. Instead the lever sat inside the plumbing, between banks, in loans that lasted one night. Nothing about the economy touched him less, apparently, and yet everything downstream of it ended up touching nobody else but him.

He tried the explanation out loud. "The Fed raises the rate banks charge each other, so borrowing costs more everywhere, so people and businesses spend less, so prices stop climbing." Elyse demurred. "You said 'everywhere.' My grandmother would ask why everywhere. You skipped a step." Leonie pointed out that he'd also said "so" four times, which made him sound like a lawnmower starting.

His mother came through the kitchen with a basket of laundry, and when she heard him rehearsing she stopped in the doorway. "Elocution," she said. "Stand up when you present. You slur when you sit." She had opinions about posture the way other people had opinions about politics, and Riley stood up, and it was humiliating how much better the sentence sounded, as though his diaphragm had been waiting years for this.

Here was what still bothered him, and he said so on the call: he could memorize the chain, demand falls, prices cool, but he could not honestly say he understood why slowing inflation required making his own car loan hypothetical. There were people who thought the whole method was a bluff, that businesses just raised prices because they could, and no interest rate would shame them into stopping. "So which is it?" Elyse asked. "Is the chain real or is it a story economists tell?" Riley said he thought it could be both. A model could be the truest thing available and still be a story. Leonie muted herself to laugh without hurting his feelings, then unmuted.

The doorbell rang while he was mid-paragraph, and it was Ms. Tanaka from next door, holding a plate of lemon bars because his mother had fixed her printer, or possibly because she wanted company, the two motives being friable in her case and crumbling into each other. Riley, still standing in presentation posture, accidentally delivered to her his entire third attempt, gestures included. She ate a lemon bar through it. When he finished, she said, "You know I worked at the Chicago Fed for thirty years."

He did not know that. She had a birdbath and a complicated relationship with the neighborhood squirrels; she had never once been a central bank. "You got it right," she said, "which puts you ahead of two of my former supervisors. The overnight part matters, by the way. Banks lend each other reserves constantly, just to balance their books. It's like breathing. The Fed makes breathing cost something." Riley asked whether the chain was real or a story. Ms. Tanaka considered the question long enough to finish the lemon bar.

"Both," she said finally. "Like most true things. You're allowed to say that to your class, as long as you say it standing up."

Back at the laptop, Elyse held the flashcard over her head. "One more time from the top. And Riley, slower on the part where you say banks charge each other. That's the part everyone gets wrong and you got it right."

He looked at the card, then at the corner of the screen where his own chin was propped on nothing. "The Fed raises the federal funds rate," he said, "which is what banks charge each other for overnight loans of reserves. And then everything else is downstream, even me."

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: At Lunar New Year, many Chinese families give money in red envelopes to children and unmarried younger relatives, because red is associated with good fortune and warding off evil.
story:
The community hall smelled of sesame oil and steam, and Layla stood near the folding tables with a red envelope in her coat pocket, turning it over and over like a coin she couldn't decide whether to spend. Ziyad's family had invited hers again this year, the way they had every winter since the two of them were seven, and the hall was already filling: paper lanterns strung along the basketball hoop, a long table of dumplings going soft in their bamboo trays, old men arguing amiably over a mahjong board in the corner. In her pocket, the envelope held a folded ten-dollar bill and her careful cursive on the back, "For Ziyad, happy new year."

She had worked it out, or thought she had. Red envelopes, she knew, were for children. She was sixteen now, tall enough that the aunties no longer pinched her cheeks, old enough that Ms. Berg had stopped calling her "one of the kids" at the library where she volunteered. So she had gone to the paper shop, asked for hongbao by pointing at a picture, and chosen envelopes printed with gold fish. If she was too old to be on the receiving end, she would join the giving end. It seemed like the mature arithmetic of the thing, a line crossed in one direction rather than refused in the other.

That morning she had messaged Ziyad, and the whole conversation was still on her phone. "Am I too old for red envelopes now," she'd typed, and then, before he answered, "Don't laugh. I'm serious." His reply had come in three bursts: "why are you asking at 8am." Then, "my cousin is 23 and unmarried and she still gets them." Then, "why, are you bringing one for me? Bring me two." She'd read the second message four times, sitting on her bed with her chin on her knees, because it opened a door she hadn't known was there. Twenty-three and unmarried and still getting them. So it wasn't only about being a child. It was something else, some arrangement of age and family and standing she couldn't see the edges of.

Ziyad found her by the tea urn, holding a can of orange soda he hadn't opened. "You actually brought one," he said. "You're going to give me money in front of my entire extended family." His great-aunt was seated near the stage like a small ascetic in a grey cardigan, taking nothing from the buffet, drinking only hot water, dispensing judgments in a dialect Layla didn't speak. "That's her," Ziyad said, lowering his voice. "She decides things." Layla watched the old woman hand a red envelope to a squirming boy of about six, press it into his palm with both hands, and say something short and firm. The boy ran off grinning. Money, red paper, and whatever she'd said, all moving together in a single gesture.

Layla took the envelope out of her pocket and offered it to Ziyad with both hands the way she'd seen the aunt do it. He was still grinning when his great-aunt appeared at his elbow, faster than a woman drinking only hot water had any right to be, and took the envelope out of the air between them. She turned it over. She read the cursive. She looked at Layla for a long, silent moment, and then she began to expostulate, waving the envelope, addressing the room, addressing Ziyad, addressing an aunt who had wandered over, until Ziyad translated, wincing: "She says you don't give to your elders. You're not married, you're the young one, it's not your turn." He paused, listening again. "She says the red is for good fortune. It keeps evil away. She wants to know why a young girl would give her money away."

The aunt returned the envelope to Layla's hand, closed Layla's fingers around it, and patted them twice, a transaction concluded. Then she reached into her own cardigan pocket and produced a second envelope, crisp and gold-flecked, and held it out. Layla looked at it and then at her own envelope in her fist, the ten dollars she'd saved from her library shift now sitting uselessly in her left hand while money arrived in her right. She took the new envelope anyway. It seemed rude to do otherwise, and besides, some part of her was already doing the arithmetic again, the arithmetic she'd gotten wrong, revising it: not too old, not a child, somewhere in the middle, eligible by a rule she hadn't written.

She sat with Ziyad at a folding table near the windows while the speeches started, her thoughts drifting tangential, away from the mayor's Mandarin pleasantries and toward the two envelopes warming her pocket. "So my ten dollars," she said finally, "I can't give it to you, and I can't keep it, because keeping would mean I think I'm done receiving, which the aunt says I'm not." Ziyad popped his soda. "Give it to the mahjong uncles as a bribe," he said. "Or the six-year-old. He'll take anything."

The six-year-old was tearing past the dessert table with a dragon mask pushed up on his forehead. Layla caught him, knelt, and held out her envelope with both hands, and he snatched it and was gone before she could finish saying happy new year. When she turned back, Ziyad's great-aunt was watching her from across the hall with an expression that was almost approval. Then she beckoned, and when Layla approached, the old woman pressed another envelope into her hands. "For next year too," Ziyad translated, shrugging. "She says to come back." Layla stood there with three envelopes in her pockets, more money than she'd brought, and heard herself say, "I came here to give one away."

activity: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
knowledge_domain: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
fact: Research by Gabriele Wulf found that learners usually improve faster when told to focus on the effect of a movement, such as the target, rather than on their own body parts.
story:
Morgan had drawn the drill on the back of a water bill: three cones, a bucket, and an arrow that was supposed to mean something. In the backyard, the cones were set up wrong twice, first by Henri, who arranged them in what he called a "sensual curve," and then by Domenic, who put one in the flowerbed and refused to move it because the dirt was, he said, already compromised. The drill itself was simple. The fourth graders on her soccer team could not pass. They kicked the ball at each other's shins, at each other's faces, occasionally at a cloud. She had one week to fix it before the season opener, and the backyard was where she planned to test her plan on her two friends, both of them seventeen and both of them terrible on purpose.

"Right," she said, jogging to the center cone. "Domenic, you're a nine-year-old. Henri, you're the ball." Henri lay down in the grass immediately, sullen as a cat in a bath, which was not what she had meant, but she let it go because it was funnier than the drill so far.

The plan was cues. On Tuesday she had written a whole sheet of them, bend your ankle, lock your ankle, follow through toward the target, and read them out like scripture while the kids got worse. Mr. Guo, watering his tomatoes over the fence, had said only one thing that evening, not as advice, just as something he'd read somewhere: that a researcher named Gabriele Wulf had found learners usually improve faster when told to focus on the effect of a movement, the ball hitting the target, instead of on their own body parts. Then he'd gone inside, leaving Morgan standing there with her useless sheet of anatomical commands and a feeling like a door had opened onto a room she'd been living next to for years.

"Okay, new rule," she said now. "Nobody says anything about ankles. Domenic, when I pass, where do you look?"

"Your feet. Obviously. It's riveting."

"Wrong. Look at my hands." She held them out, and Domenic, still sulking over his compromised dirt, mirrored her without complaint. She pushed a firm pass straight into his palms. The ball thumped satisfyingly against skin. "See? I'm not aiming at you. I'm aiming at your hands."

"That's it? That's the whole revolution?"

"That's the whole revolution."

Henri sat up, brushing grass off his elbows. "So all week you were telling kids to think about their wrists, and Wulf's research says the opposite, that they improve faster focusing on the effect, like the target, rather than their own body parts, and you've only just now sensitize ... sensitized yourself to this?" He grinned. "Sensitized. I've been saving that one since the SAT booklet."

"You used it wrong and you know it."

"I used it beautifully and you're jealous."

They ran the drill for real then, Morgan passing, Domenic catching, Henri eventually standing in as a miniature defender with his arms crossed like a tiny furious bouncer. Between rounds Morgan kept a tally in her head. Passes that hit hands: better than her Tuesday session, though with a sample size of two seventeen-year-olds pretending to be nine, which was, she admitted to herself, not science. Maybe the improvement was the cue. Maybe Domenic just liked being told what to look at instead of what to fix, since he spent all day at school being told what to fix. She couldn't separate those yet. She wrote both possibilities on the water bill, under the arrow.

"What's that column," Domenic said, peering over her shoulder, "the one marked economics?"

"That's where I keep my doubts."

"Label it stagflation, then. Doubts that keep growing while nothing else does."

Henri pointed at him. "That one you used correctly, unfortunately."

On Saturday, the fourth graders arrived at the field like a herd of small sullen buffalo who had been told soccer was a punishment. Morgan set the cones, held up her hands, and said nothing about ankles at all. "Every pass," she told them, "hits your teammate's hands. That's the whole game today. Hands, hands, hands." By the third drill, a girl named nothing Morgan needed to remember was hitting hands she wasn't even looking at, and a boy who had spent Tuesday weeping near the goal was shouting "hands" like a war cry, and the team, briefly, looked like a team.

She stood at the edge of the cones with the water bill folded in her pocket, still holding both columns open. After the session she texted Mr. Guo a photo of the tally, and he replied with a thumbs up and nothing else, which was, she decided, the correct amount.

"Again," shouted the weeping boy, dragging the ball back to the center cone. "Make it harder this time."

Morgan jogged out and held up her hands.

activity: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
knowledge_domain: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
fact: Schenck v. United States introduced the 'clear and present danger' test, allowing speech to be punished if it created a clear and present danger of harm Congress could prevent.
story:
Ryan spread the case files across his grandfather's kitchen table, the same table where, every Sunday of his childhood, pancakes had been served on a plate with a chip in the rim. His grandfather watched from the doorway with a dish towel over his shoulder, saying nothing, which Ryan had learned was an invitation rather than an absence.

The assignment had seemed simple when Mr. Joseph announced it: argue both sides of a free speech case before a mock court, first for the student who had been suspended for a viral post, then for the school that suspended him. Two weeks of preparation. Ryan had assumed the hard part would be memorizing arguments. Instead he kept discovering that every argument he built for one side dismantled something he believed about the other, and by Thursday night he had stopped sleeping well.

"You're chewing that pen like it owes you money," his grandfather said, setting down two mugs of tea. "Impecunious fellows chew like that."

"I have to argue the school's side tomorrow," Ryan said, "and I don't believe the school's side. The post was ugly, but it was just a post. Nobody got hurt." He slid a printout across the table. "But there's this. Schenck versus United States. The Court said speech can be punished if it creates a clear and present danger of harm Congress could prevent. That's the test, or it was. If I'm the school's lawyer, I say the post was a danger, clear and present, and I win."

His grandfather pulled reading glasses from his shirt pocket and bent over the page. In the next room the clock his grandmother had wound for forty years ticked on, and Ryan could hear his own pulse in his ears, the way it had gone before every debate round that year.

"Look at the second page," Ryan said. "Wade sent it. He's arguing against me, and he's going to say the test is a fossil. He already told me he would. He said Schenck came from a war case, pamphlets, espionage, that nobody applies it like that anymore, that later Courts tightened it up until 'clear and present danger' barely means anything." He heard the bitterness in his own voice and was embarrassed by it, because Wade was right and Wade knew it, and Wade had texted him the citation at eleven at night with a single thumbs up, which was either mercy or taunting.

His grandfather read for a long moment. "When I was your age," he said, "I argued with my father about the Vietnam War at this table. He was for it, I was against it, and we both lost our tempers. Took me thirty years to understand he wasn't wrong about everything and I wasn't right about everything. We were just each holding half." He tapped the printout. "So your friend says the test is old. What do you say back?"

Ryan had been ruminating on that question all week, turning it over on the bus, in the shower, during a chemistry test he had probably failed. "That's what I can't figure out," he said. "If I say the test is still good, I'm arguing that a school can punish speech it thinks is dangerous, and that could swallow everything, every unpopular thing anyone ever posted. But if I say the test is dead, then I'm saying the school can never act until somebody actually gets hurt, and that's insane too. Somebody gets hurt, and then what, the principal writes an apology?" He pushed the papers away. "In ethics class we read about utilitarianism. Greatest good for the greatest number. Mr. Joseph keeps asking whether punishing one kid's speech is worth preventing harm to a hundred others, and I keep wanting to answer yes and no at the same time."

"So answer both," his grandfather said. It was not quite advice; it sounded more like something the old man had been waiting all evening to say. He drank his tea and looked at the window, where the porch light made a yellow square on the grass.

Ryan sat with that. He pulled the papers back and began writing, not notes for one side or the other but a single page with a line drawn down the middle. On the left he wrote the school's claim: the post created a danger, clear and present, a danger of harm Congress could prevent, and that was enough to punish it. On the right he wrote Wade's answer: the test came from another era, and treating it as settled law was like navigating by a map of a country that had rearranged itself. Then, at the bottom, below both columns, he wrote a sentence he did not show his grandfather: the honest position is that the line between dangerous speech and merely offensive speech has never been drawn straight, and maybe the arguing is the line.

The next afternoon the mock court convened in Mr. Joseph's room, and Wade went first, smooth and confident, calling the old test outdated in his opening breath. When Ryan rose for the school, he did not deny it. He stood at the front with his grandfather's phrase in his head like a coin in his pocket, and he heard himself say, "My opponent is right that the test is old. I'm asking you to decide whether old means wrong." The panel leaned forward. Wade's eyebrows went up, and then, slowly, he smiled, the smile of someone who realized the round had just become worth playing.

After class Mr. Joseph stopped Ryan at the door. "You didn't win," he said. "The panel split two to one against you. But that last exchange was the best argument I've heard all semester." Ryan found Wade already at the lockers, holding out his phone with the group chat open, where Brian had typed a single message: rematch. Ryan typed back, "My grandfather's table. Sunday. Bring the later cases."

activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
knowledge_domain: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
fact: New Zealand was the first country to adopt formal inflation targeting, when its government and Reserve Bank agreed in March 1990 on a target range of 0 to 2 percent.
story:
The market opened at eight, and by ten the gravel lot behind the elementary school had filled with folding tables of tomatoes, bread, jars of honey labeled in someone's grandmother's handwriting. Lea carried a notebook she had filled on the bus, and the notebook was the problem. Her orientation advisor at the college had emailed on Thursday: every incoming scholarship student had to give a three-minute explanation of a policy concept at the welcome brunch on Sunday, and Lea had drawn the topic from a hat she now suspected was rigged. How a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation. She had until two o'clock tomorrow, and everything she had written sounded like a Wikipedia article read aloud.

She found Tatiana at the bread table, hands dusted with flour because Tatiana's mother sold the loaves and Tatiana lugged them from the van. "Say it to me again," Tatiana said, wrapping a sourdough in paper. "You practiced on the bus, right?"

"That's the thing. I can recite it and I don't understand it, and I can tell the difference now, which is worse." Lea flipped the notebook open to a page of arrows. "The bank raises rates, borrowing costs more, people buy less, prices stop climbing so fast. Fine. But why would a bank want to control prices at all? Who gave it that job? That's the part everyone skips."

Noemy arrived with a bag of plums and split it three ways while they walked the rows. Noemy was going to community college in the fall to study accounting, and she liked problems that had answers, so she frowned at Lea's notebook the way she frowned at a receipt that wouldn't balance. "Maybe nobody gave it the job. Maybe it just started doing it and kept going."

"Someone had to decide first, though. Some country had to be first." Lea stopped between a table of alluvial soil-darkened carrots and a cooler of trout, and took out her phone, thumbing past messages from her mother asking if she'd eaten. Noemy leaned on a crate to wait, chewing a plum, spitting the pit into her palm.

Lea found it on a central bank history page, squinting against the sun. "New Zealand," she said. "It was New Zealand. In March 1990, their government and their Reserve Bank agreed on a target range, zero to two percent. Inflation targeting. That's what it's called." She read the line twice to fix it. "So before that, banks weren't aiming at a set number at all. Someone had to invent the target, and it was them."

"Okay," Tatiana said, "so the target is like the price tag on the bread. The bank isn't the bread, it's the tag."

It wasn't like that, exactly, and Lea was about to say so when Ms. Popal, who kept the flower stall at the end of the row and had apparently been listening, set down her shears. She didn't explain. She said, "Tell me why you care, and I'll tell you whether I believe you," and turned back to her buckets of dahlias as if the whole thing bored her, which was clearly a test of some kind, an artifice Lea recognized because her grandmother did the same thing with the good china.

"Because my mom's rent went up and her wages didn't," Lea said, surprised at herself. "And everyone argues about whose fault it is, and I want to be able to follow the argument instead of just having a feeling about it. Prices rising too fast hurts her. The bank's tool might help, or might push us into losing jobs, and I can hold both of those at once. That's all I've got."

Ms. Popal considered a dahlia, cut it, and handed it over without a word, which Lea took as passing. Noemy said, "That's more than three minutes' worth," and Tatiana said, "It's a better three minutes than the arrows."

They sat on the tailgate of the bread van and Lea rebuilt the talk out loud, using what was around her. She started with the New Zealand fact, the first target, March 1990, the zero to two percent range, because it gave the whole thing a beginning, a moment when someone wrote a number down and made the bank responsible to it. Then she moved to the mechanism she had recited all morning, but slower now, stitched to the market around them, the vendors, the customers counting change. She still didn't know, honestly, whether the tool worked as cleanly as the textbooks claimed, or who bore the cost when it worked, and she said so in her closing line, because Noemy had pointed out that admitting the seam was stronger than pretending there wasn't one. Lea liked that; the talk had a suture in it now, visible, deliberate.

At two she would rehearse once more in her kitchen, and tomorrow she would stand up with dahlia still on the counter at home. For now she bought the tomatoes, counted her change, and said, "Okay, from the top, one more time, and time me."

story:
The check lay on the kitchen table of his grandfather's house, folded once, and Tyler kept smoothing the crease while his grandmother moved between the stove and the window. Two hundred and twelve dollars, his first real paycheck from the grocery store, and an amp he'd been circling online for weeks. Scarlet had a birthday coming up too, and Koraly kept saying they should all pitch in for the party. The money was already spent in three directions before he'd cashed it.

"You're quiet," his grandmother said. She set down a plate of bread and did not sit, because she never sat when there was daylight left. "Go look at the porch railing before you leave. Your grandfather's list is on the bench, and half of it I can't lift."

The list was in pencil, cramped, item after item, and Tyler recognized the handwriting from birthday cards. His grandfather had been dead since March, and the house still ran on his notes, which was either very sad or very organized, depending on how you looked at it. The railing was the third item. Tyler tested it, and a spindle came away in his hand, dry-rotted clean through, light as a wasp nest.

In the workshop off the garage he found the calculator in the same drawer where the pencil sharpener had always lived. He wasn't looking for it; he was looking for the drill. But he sat down on the stool with the spindle in his lap and, because the amp was on his mind, he started doing arithmetic. The amp cost four hundred. If he saved instead, put a thousand away and left it, his economics teacher had mentioned seven percent once, in passing, as though it were a rumor. Tyler typed it out, multiplying year by year, and had to start over twice because his thumb slipped. At the third try the numbers began to double back on themselves in a way that felt like a trick. Forty years, because he was eighteen now, would put him at fifty-eight.

He carried the calculator inside, holding it the way you hold a thing you don't quite believe. "Grandma. A thousand dollars, seven percent a year. In forty years it's almost fifteen thousand."

She looked at the little screen and then at him. "So money you save at eighteen grows a lot of times over by the time you retire." She said it plainly, the way she repeated weather forecasts. Then she went back to stirring, and added, "Your grandfather would call that a pithy argument for boring habits."

Tyler sat with that. His grandfather had done exactly that, apparently; there was a folder in the desk drawer with bank statements going back decades, and Tyler remembered being small and bored at this same table while the numbers were discussed. He'd thought of it then as a life spent prognosticating about a future that never arrived, a man always preparing for a day he was too careful to enjoy. But the railing, the list, the paid-off house, the folder: the future had arrived, and it looked like this. Tyler tried to hold both pictures at once, the man who wouldn't buy the good coffee and the man whose wife had a roof and a garden and bread on the table in March, and he couldn't get them to be the same man or a different one. Maybe both. He let it stay uncertain, because it was.

Koraly texted him a photo of the amp screenshot with the caption your move. Scarlet wanted a bonfire at the quarry, and Tyler wanted to be there, wanted the amp, wanted the summer to sound like something. He typed back not sure yet, which was true in both directions.

He went back out to the porch with the drill and the spindle and a scrap of cedar his grandfather had saved in the rafters for no reason Tyler had understood until now. The light was going amber over the neighbor's fence, and Ms. Ross, next door, called out that if he was fixing that railing she had one just like it, and she'd pay him in tomatoes. He worked until the new spindle sat flush and solid under his palm, and inside his head he ran the number again, a thousand to almost fifteen thousand, forty years, and put the drill down and texted his dad: coming Sunday, I'll help clean out the garage if you want.

His grandmother came out with iced tea for both of them and stood at the top of the steps, one hand on the rail he'd just mended, testing it.

"Solid," Tyler said.

She squeezed it once more, satisfied. "Ms. Ross," she called across the fence, "he does fences too."
